paragraphs.text: LEO THE GRAMMARIAN'S [CHRONICLE] CONTAINING THE [REIGNS OF THE] NEW EMPERORS. Leo the Armenian, the apostate, reigned for [?] years and 5 months. He was crowned by Patriarch Nikephoros, after giving him a written assurance of his own orthodoxy. Krum, the new Sennacherib, puffed up by his victory, left his own brother to besiege Adrianople. Six days into Leo's reign he came back to the City and went around in front of the walls [?] … the Chronography of the New Emperors [?] of Leo the Grammarian, on the 8th of July, the feast of the holy great martyr Procopius, in the year [?], and duke of the Cibyrrhaeots [?] Tzikandelos [?] … [?] man of our mighty and first emperor [?] … for this [?] to the author [?]

from Blachernae as far as the gate called the Golden Gate, showing off his power. In the meadow by the Golden Gate he performed foul sacrifices. He demanded that the emperor either make peace or let him plant his spear in the Golden Gate. When the emperor refused, he went back to his own tent, struck with wonder at the walls of the city and the emperor's well-ordered battle line. So he turned to a peace agreement, making proposals meant to test the emperor. The emperor seized the opportunity and tried to ambush him. But he was kept from carrying the plan through by the cowardice of the men who did the work: they wounded Krum, but did not deal him a fatal blow. Enraged at this, the fiend sent horsemen to St Mamas and burned the palace there. He loaded onto wagons the bronze lion of the hippodrome, together with the bear and the dragon of the fountain and some very fine marbles, and went back. He laid siege to Adrianople and took it. Then he carried many of the Macedonian nobles across, together with a great many of the common people, and settled them by the Danube.

After two years of his reign Leo went mad. He exiled the divine Nikephoros, who had crowned him, and in his place appointed Theodotos as patriarch, a man without reason and more speechless than the fish. He also fanned into flame a relentless persecution against the Church. In his time a comet appeared in the shape of two bright moons, which joined together and then split again into various shapes, until it took the form of a headless man. Fearful earthquakes, droughts and scorching heat also came in the days of this God-hated man. Imitating his namesake, a man of the same character who had founded this foul heresy, he set the heresy going again. Then he went looking for fellow initiates. He found John, called the Grammarian, or rather a second Jannes or Simon, notorious for divining with bowls, for sorcery and for obscene practices, and some others of like mind. So he summoned Nikephoros, the patriarch of blessed memory, and the bishops with him before the senate, and said: "Know for certain that some people have arisen who say that the icons ought not to be venerated." At once the holy Euthymios of Sardis spoke out boldly from divine Scripture and rebuked the scoundrel. After him Theodore, abbot of the Stoudios and a fervent champion of orthodoxy, said: "Emperor, do not unsettle the order of the Church. Yours is the ordering of the state and the command of the army; take care of these, and let the Church remain in orthodoxy." On hearing this the tyrant boiled over with rage, and the little ape let out a lion's roar. He drove them all out with insults, expelled the great Nikephoros from the city and confined him. Likewise he exiled Theo-

dore of the Stoudios, and he installed Theodotos Kassiteras in the patriarchate. From then on he poured out the rage and cunning of his soul and entrusted himself to his licentious fellow initiates. Once they had become his intimates, they put three things before him which they had promised and which pleased him: the denial of our orthodox faith, the destruction of the divine icons, and the persecution of the pious. The empty-headed man gave his assent to these deceptions, and the wretch, given wings by his miserable impulse, first took down every sacred image set up in the church. After that he condemned anyone found with icons of Christ or of any saint to terrible punishments and to death, and he killed many distinguished and eminent men. Michael, who held command of the Excubitors regiment, was slandered to the emperor as plotting against him, and the emperor kept him in fetters under guard in prison. When the Nativity of our Savior came round, he wanted to kill him that night, but his own wife stopped him because of the feast, and he let him be. Michael learned of this in prison and sent word to all his fellow conspirators: "Unless you hurry to get me out of custody, I will denounce every one of you to the emperor." Among them was also the papias of the palace, a relative of Michael. That night they armed themselves, carrying their swords under their clothes. The papias opened the doors, and they went in dressed as priests in their vestments. When the emperor entered the church, they sprang on him, seized him and hacked him limb from limb. So he breathed out his unholy soul in the palace, where none of those who had reigned before him had ever been killed. In that same hour they went to the prison, brought Michael out and led him into the feast, now wearing a crown instead of chains. So the word of the psalm was fulfilled in him: "In the evening weeping will lodge, and in the morning rejoicing." After this they wrapped the scoundrel's body in cheap rags, threw his utterly foul limbs into a small boat and carried them off to the island called Prote. There they also tonsured his sons and made them become monks.

with prisons, punishments and exiles, [?] dreaming of freedom and relief as in a dream. But he cherished the God-hated [heresy] of his impious predecessor, for out of utter folly and ignorance he too was caught on the same hook of terrible heresy. So at a silention he said: "Those before us who examined the Church's rule of doctrine will give account for it, whether they decreed well or badly. We prefer to keep the Church on the path on which we found it walking." He had a son by Euphrosyne named Theophilos, whom he crowned in the Great Church. In his time Thomas the rebel set out from the eastern regions, dragging along a mixed rabble. Being low-born and obscure, he went to the regions of Syria, calling himself Constantine, son of Empress Irene. From there he deceived many of the barbarians into turning against Christians and gathered a countless host. Then he marched against Constantinople, boasting of the size of his army and not considering that a king is not saved by great power. He besieged Constantinople for one year, while the citizens resisted bravely, fighting from the walls and at sea. They burned most of his ships and routed the enemy's picked troops. At a loss, he abandoned the City and went off to Thrace, plundering it. Michael slipped out of the City with a very large force and set out against him. He besieged him for a short time and captured him without effort. He cut off his hands and feet and then impaled him. So he ended the grievous civil war that Thomas had started and kept going for three years. While Michael was busy with the rebel Thomas and neglected everything else in his concern for this, Crete, Sicily and the islands called the Cyclades were torn away from the dominion of the Romans by Africans and Arabs. Because of the people's sins and the impiety of the rulers, they then began for the first time both to humble the affairs of the Christians and to bring them under their hand [?]. While matters stood thus, Michael died a wretched death from a disease of the bladder and pain in the kidneys. His son Theophilos took over the rule in his place, together with his mother Euphrosyne. [?] and dragging along a mixed [rabble], he moved against Byzantium, aiming at the empire beyond his worth; for setting out from the land of the Romans, low-born [?] …

Theophilos reigned for 12 years. His mother Euphrosyne sent to all the themes and brought in beautiful maidens so that she could choose a bride for her son Theophilos. She brought them into the palace, into the hall called the Pearl, and gave Theophilos a golden apple, saying: "Give this to whichever one pleases you." Among them was a girl of noble family named Ikasia, extremely beautiful. When Theophilos saw her he greatly admired her beauty and said: "So it was through a woman that evils flowed." She answered with a certain modesty: "But it is also through a woman that better things spring forth." Stung to the heart by her reply, he passed her over and gave the apple to Theodora, who came from Paphlagonia. He crowned Theodora in the oratory of St Stephen, and he himself was crowned together with her by Patriarch Antony. On holy Pentecost he went in procession to the holy Great Church and bestowed a great deal of money on the patriarch, as well as on the clergy and the senate. Ikasia, having missed the throne, built a monastery. There she took the veil and lived on in asceticism and philosophy, living for God alone, until the end of her life. She also left behind a great many writings. The emperor's mother Euphrosyne left the palace of her own accord and lived in quiet in her monastery, called ta Gastria. Theophilos held horse races and ordered his protovestiarios Leo Chamodrakon to bring the chandelier that had been hacked by a sword when Leo the Armenian was slain. When the races were over he summoned the whole senate to the place called the Kathisma. He brought out the chandelier, showed it to them and said: "He who enters a temple of the Lord and murders the Lord's anointed: of what is he guilty?" The senate answered: "He is guilty of death, O master." At once he ordered the eparch to arrest those who had killed Leo together with his father Michael and to cut off their heads in the Sphendone. They protested loudly, saying that such a judgment was unjust: "For if we had not fought alongside your father, you would not be reigning as emperor now." And so they were beheaded in front of everyone. The pretext was that they had dared to commit murder in a temple of the Lord. In truth it was because they had killed his fellow heretic, a man of one mind with him in impiety. For the scoundrel held to that man's God-hated heresy, pulling down some of the holy icons and digging out others. Theophobos the Persian fled to this Theophilos together with his father and 14,000 Persians. Theophilos distributed them among the themes, settled them there and organized them into tourmai,

which to this day are called the Persian tourmai. Theophobos himself he made his brother-in-law by marrying him to a sister of Theodora Augusta. Theophilos loved splendor. Through the head of the goldsmiths' workshop, a very learned man and a relative of Patriarch Antony, he had the Pentapyrgion made, and the two great organs of solid gold, which he adorned with various stones and glass. He also had a golden tree made, in which perching birds sang musically by some mechanism. He also refashioned the imperial robes, renewing them, along with their gold-woven ornaments. He made a show of worldly justice, though he wronged the faith and piety more than the emperors before him. At Blachernae a widow approached him and cried out that she was being wronged by Petronas, the Augusta's brother and droungarios of the Watch [?]: "He is raising his own buildings higher and doing me harm with them. He blocks the light from mine and makes them worthless, as if I were a despised widow." Those who went saw this injustice and confirmed that what the woman said was true, and they returned and reported it to the emperor. Petronas was convicted by them, stripped in the middle of the street and flogged hard on the back. The quaestor and the antigrapheis were ordered to go and raze his buildings to the foundations and hand over [the site] to the woman. This emperor took Alexios the Armenian, surnamed Mousele, a brave and strong man, as son-in-law for his beloved daughter Maria. He made him a patrician and shortly afterward a magistros. Then he came to suspect him of aspiring to the throne and sent him out as general and duke of Sicily. Since envy was at work, some Sicilians came up and slandered him to the emperor, saying that he was betraying the Christians' interests to the Hagarenes and plotting against the throne. Meanwhile Maria, the emperor's beloved daughter, died. He adorned her sarcophagus with silver and granted a charter of immunity to anyone who took refuge there on any charge. (Emperor Leo later took this silver from the tomb.) At the time of the slander against Alexios, Theodore the archbishop, called Krithinos, was in the City. The emperor summoned him, gave him his own reliquary, and sent him to Sicily to give Alexios a pledge of safety and bring him back. Theodore went and, by his natural intelligence, persuaded Alexios and brought him to the emperor. The emperor beat him as a rebel and put him in prison, confiscating all his property. And when the emperor
[?] Combefis's notes [?]. … honoring him with the rank of patrician and anthypatos because of [his] affection for his daughter, and then ma-

[with a] loud [voice] the archbishop cried out: "Go forth and prosper, and reign!" [And he added:] "For the sake of what, O emperor?" The emperor, feeling shamed before the senate, said: "For the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness." The archbishop replied: "And what righteousness is there in you? Through me you gave Alexios a signed pledge, and you did not keep it." The emperor felt himself convicted. Moved by uncontrollable anger and rage, he dragged the archbishop violently from the altar, gave him a severe beating and sent him into exile. He did this not only because he had been rebuked by him, but also because he had found out that the archbishop honored and revered the holy icons and secretly denounced the emperor's impiety. Not long afterward the emperor came to the Great Church, and the patriarch reproached him over the bishop, so he brought him back with an apology. But the bishop judged himself unworthy of the priesthood because of what he had suffered, so the emperor made him oikonomos of the Great Church. He also had Alexios released from prison, gave him back all his property and held him in honor. Manuel was the most renowned soldier of all the men in the East whom the emperor honored. He had exchanged some words with Myron, who was logothete of the drome and father-in-law of Petronas. At Myron's instigation he was slandered to the emperor as aspiring to the throne, and dire plans were laid against him. Leo the protovestiarios took Manuel's side and looked after him, assuring the emperor again and again that what was said against him was false. When Manuel learned of all this, he slipped out of the City to escape the emperor's anger and the slanders. He went as far as the gates, mounted the public post-horses and fled as far as the passes of Syria, hamstringing the horses as he went. He sent this message to the Hagarenes: "I am fleeing the emperor's anger. If you will not force me to abandon my faith, I will take refuge with you. If you will receive me on these terms, send me a pledge of safety." They took this as a great favor, sent the pledge and received him as if he were an emperor of the Romans. When the emperor learned that Manuel had gone over to the Hagarenes, he fell into great distress and anguish, and he took counsel with John the synkellos about it. John said: "If you truly want Manuel to come back to you, O emperor, I myself am ready to do it. I will take money and be sent to the amermoumnes, supposedly [?] … 'with an apology' [?] …

to visit those in prison. With a signed pledge from Your Majesty I will persuade Manuel to come to you. I expect to accomplish this both with the signed pledge and with my own powers of persuasion." The emperor gave him a great deal of money and gifts for the amermoumnes and sent him off. John arrived with much money and all kinds of finery, so that even the Hagarenes were astonished at his wealth. He distributed alms in the prisons, met the chief counselor, and was even able to talk with Manuel in secret. He gave him the signed pledge and the emperor's reliquary. When he had done this, he returned and reported to the emperor all that he had accomplished. Manuel asked the amermoumnes to let him march out against a nation that was hostile to them, and his request was granted. He took the amermoumnes's son and a large army, went off and won a great victory. Because of this he was raised to even higher honor than before and had complete influence with the amermoumnes. Since he was very anxious to get away to Romania, after some time he said to the amermoumnes's magnates: "If you give me the amermoumnes's son and an army, I will go out and subdue Romania." They were overjoyed at this, and because of his earlier success they armed him at once and sent him against Romania. When he came near the theme of the Anatolics, he called together the men under his command and the amermoumnes's son, as if for exercise and hunting. Once he was far from the enemy [?], he embraced the amermoumnes's son, kissed him and said: "I am going away to the emperor and my own people. You go back to your own people with your men, and do not fear any harm from us." And so the son returned in tears and shame. Manuel went on toward the emperor, sending ahead someone to announce his coming. The emperor rewarded the messenger with money and honors and received Manuel as he deserved. He made him magistros and domestic of the scholai at once and stood sponsor for his children at holy baptism. Encouraged by this, the emperor marched out with Manuel and the senate against the Hagarenes, and easily [?] both Zapetra and Samosata, abounding then in wealth and power through the amermoumnes, from there [?] … [?] the chrysobull was given [?] … the amermoumnes's homeland, from there [?] … having taken Zapetra by siege [?] … [?]

[?] … and exulting in the spoils. When he reached Bryas, he ordered a palace to be built there, parks to be planted and water to be brought in, and this was done. From there he came to the City and celebrated a triumph with the spoils. He held horse races and drove the first race himself, riding a white chariot and dressed in the Blue color. He won and was crowned, while the demes shouted: "Welcome, incomparable charioteer!" When Patriarch Antony died, John the synkellos was ordained in his place: a new Jannes and Jambres, so to speak, notorious for divinations, for divining with bowls and for every impiety. He proved a fitting tool for the emperor's impiety and inclinations, and he worked with him in everything that led to perdition. The emperor had long been in labor with the basilisk of impiety but had held it in; now he let it burst out and brought it to birth, ordering the holy icons to be smeared over or scraped off. Outside the City this John built a house of hewn stone, which to this day is called Trullos. There he conversed with demons by means of certain sacrifices and revealed the future to the emperor. The house remained uninhabited because of the visits of demons that took place in it at that time. While things stood thus, the Arabs marched against Romania in great force. The emperor went out against them with the Persian refugees and Manuel the domestic. When battle was joined, the emperor was defeated and went into the midst of the Persians so that they might save him. But Manuel learned that the emperor was among the Persians and that they already meant to betray him to the Arabs and make their peace with them through him. He cut his way through them, took hold of the emperor's bridle in their midst and came out leading him. He thought it an intolerable disgrace for the Romans if the Arabs took the emperor of the Romans captive. Afraid of the situation he was in [?], the emperor wanted to run back to the Persians, but Manuel raised his sword as if to strike him down. The emperor took fright and followed against his will, … [?] … urging Theophilos to withdraw [?] … nor to depict these with colors and to give them shape [?] … [?] … and a third time, from the right [?], he cut through the phalanx surrounding the emperor and came close to him, so that he mounted the one carrying him on a horse and again managed to rescue him [?]. When not even on the second attempt did the matter succeed [?] …

…having been saved, he turned back from there to Dorylaeum in shame and after a heavy defeat. Manuel had been wounded in the battle. He fell ill and died, after showing great valour against the Hagarenes. His body was brought back and laid in the monastery he had built, the one called Manuel's, near the cistern of Aspar. And at once slanders against the Persians reached the emperor. At that time a son was born to the emperor by Theodora, and he named him Michael.

As the emperor was on his way to Blachernae, a man came up to him and said, "The horse Your Majesty is riding is mine." The horse was prancing, and when the emperor had reined it in he asked the count of the stable, "Whose horse is this?" He said, "The count of the Opsikion sent it to Your Majesty." Since the count of the Opsikion was in the City, the next day the emperor brought him in together with the man who had approached him and said, "Tell the truth: whose horse is this?" The man answered, "It was mine. The general sent men and took it from me by force, without paying me a price or even asking me." The emperor said to the count, "Tell me, is this so? And why did you send me the horse without settling a price for it?" He said, "Because he was seeking to become a scholarios. Since I did not know whether he was brave, I offered him a hundred nomismata, but he would not take them." The emperor investigated and was satisfied that the general had taken the horse by force. He chastised the general with the proper floggings and returned the horse to the man who had approached him. But the man did not want it, and took two pounds of gold for it instead. The general was ordered to test him, and if he proved brave, to make him a scholarios. The man went off to war, and in the battle [?] he was found among those who fled and was cut down.

When the emperor had gone out in procession to Bryas, a message reached him from the [general] of the Anatolikoi that the protosymboulos had set out with a great host and was on his way to sack Amorium. The emperor gave the customary payments to the army and the officers and marched out swiftly as far as Cappadocia. The caliph detached eight thousand men, put at their head Souoem [?], who was most renowned among the Hagarenes for courage and judgement, and sent them against the emperor. Battle was joined, and the emperor was defeated and fled. He returned in shame, barely saved. The caliph then advanced with a great force, threw a palisade around Amorium, and fought many battles, but he could not take it, for those inside fought nobly and steadfastly. A certain [disciple] of Leo the Philosopher was in the fortress [?] [the rest of the paragraph is garbled]

…[when the caliph was about] to withdraw, this same astronomer sent word through someone: "If you hold out at the fortress for two days, you will take us." And that is what happened, for it was betrayed by the man called Boiditzes and by the Manichaean-eater [?]. Among those captured and taken off to Syria as prisoners were renowned men of no mean birth: [?] the patrician; the generals Melissenos and Aetios; Theodore the protospatharios, Krateros; Kallistos the tourmarches; Cyril the droungarios; Bassoes; and certain officers of the tagmata. The protosymboulos tried to force them to deny their faith. When he could not persuade them, their heads were cut off with the sword, for they loved eternal life above this passing one.

But the disciple of Leo the Philosopher, who had traded that noblest end for a shameful safety, went over to the caliph and was questioned by him about his learning. He said he was a disciple of Leo the Philosopher. [The caliph asked] who this Leo was, and was eager to see what sort of man he might be. So he gave one of the captives a letter for Leo the Philosopher and sent him to Constantinople, promising Leo that if he would come to him he would be held in honour. When Leo received the letter he was afraid that it might be discovered, and he took it to the emperor Theophilus. The emperor, learning of Leo's learning, took him into his service and kept him in the palace of the Magnaura. He assigned him students to teach and supplied everything he needed for his work. This Leo also became metropolitan of Thessalonica.

This same emperor built the Triconch in the palace, the so-called Sigma, and the stepped stands where the factions take their places, and a fountain at which the so-called Saximodeximon [?] takes place, when the horses of both parties pass by in golden trappings. Beneath the Triconch he made, by a mechanical device, the so-called Mystery, in which whatever someone says in one corner can be heard in the other.

This Theophilus learned that Theophanes the poet and his brother Theodore, living privately by themselves, were mocking and denouncing his impiety. In anger he sent for them and had them brought before him, and said: "Where are you from?" They said, "From where? From Palestine." The wretch said, "And why, when you have left your own land and come to ours, do you not obey Our Majesty?" When they made no answer, he ordered their [faces] to be struck violently. After this he had them flogged with ox-sinews in his rage almost to the point of death, and said in a harsh voice to the eparch, "Take them to the [praetorium]." [A garbled passage follows, apparently describing the fountain at the time of the dexima: not with pistachios and almonds, but filled with spiced wine flowing from a [?] … he mixed for all and offered it … to those standing there [?].]

…praetorium, and write these iambic verses [?] on their faces." And he added, "Even if they are not good verses, never mind." He said this because he knew they were very learned and superbly trained. They said, "Write, write, emperor, whatever you please, since you will come to know it before the fearsome Judge." The eparch took them to the praetorium, and after two days he stretched them out, bound their hands and feet, pricked the verses into their [faces], engraved them there, and sent them into exile. Theodore, now among the saints, died in exile. But the celebrated Theophanes the poet survived until the reign of Michael and Theodora. He struggled greatly in the restoration of Orthodoxy that then took place, and he became metropolitan of Nicaea once affairs had been restored to a more pious state.

In Theophilus' reign the golden plume fell from the statue of Justinian in the so-called Augusteion. Everyone was at a loss and was considering how to get up there, when a craftsman who worked on scaffolding was found. He climbed onto the roof tiles of the Great Church and shot an arrow with a rope attached at the horseman of Justinian. When the arrow had lodged there, he ran across along the rope, to the amazement of those watching, and fixed the plume back in place. He won the emperor's favour and was rewarded by the emperor with a hundred nomismata.

Theophilus crowned his son Michael in the Great Church. He also built a hospice, the one now called Ta Theophilou. Before his death this God-hated emperor held a great council with men of his own mind about Theophobos the Persian: the Persians under him held him in great affection, and he feared that once he himself had died they might plot a usurpation against his son, who was still an infant, and against his wife. So he sent for Theophobos, brought him to the palace and kept him by his side. When his illness grew heavy he imprisoned Theophobos in the vaults of the Boukoleon. The Persians asked after him and what had become of him. The emperor sent Petronas, the Augusta's brother, together with the logothete, and had Theophobos beheaded. These two persuaded the Persians that he was with the emperor in the palace. When the emperor had miserably given up his soul to dysentery, his wretched body was carried to the Holy Apostles. They secretly brought the body of Theophobos out through the Boukoleon and kept it safe near the house of Narses, in what is now called the monastery of Theophobia [?], and there they laid it to rest.

…four. Theodora was so faithful and orthodox that even while her husband was still alive she secretly honoured and venerated the holy icons. On her own judgement, but also on the advice and urging of Theoktistos, the kanikleios and logothete, she drove the patriarch John, who was her [kinsman?] [?], out of the church and out of the City, confining him to the Stenon, at the place called Kleidion. She brought in Methodios, now among the saints, who was a monk, and installed him as patriarch. She brought back together all the monks and bishops whom Theophilus had exiled, confirmed the orthodox faith, and gave the Church peace.

On the first Sunday of holy Lent she sent Theoktistos the logothete against Crete. He set out with a great host and a large fleet and badly frightened the Hagarenes, but was himself still more badly frightened and chose to flee, having heard that the Augusta had appointed another emperor. This rumour, by the cunning of the Saracens and the [?] of those with him, alarmed him and persuaded him to return to the City and abandon the army, which then fell to the swords of the men in Crete. So disgracefully did he show himself in Crete. And when Amer then marched against Romania, plundering and wrecking everything in his path, Theodora and Michael again sent the same Theoktistos against Amer with a large force, since he was the most loyal and closest to them. He arrived and joined battle with Amer [?] … because of the logothete's harshness and the hatred he inspired. One of these was Theophanes from Pharganoi, who surpassed many in courage and strength. Later, having received a promise of immunity, he fled over to the Christians.

By now the emperor had come of age and spent his time on hunting, on horse races in the diaulos of the Hippodrome, and on other impure pursuits. So Theodora Augusta took counsel with Theoktistos the logothete about giving her son a wife. For she knew he had formed an attachment to Eudokia, Inger's daughter, whom the logothete and the empress greatly disliked for her shamelessness. Therefore they married him to Eudokia, the daughter of Dekapolites, and he was crowned with her in the church of St Stephen in the Daphne. The bridal chamber was prepared in the Magnaura, and the senate reclined at the Nineteen Couches.

A little later the general of the Boukellarioi brought the emperor a spirited and noble horse. Wanting to harness it for the Hippodrome, the emperor wished to examine its [teeth] [? garbled marginal notes follow: "brought peace to the Church on the first Sunday"; "Theoktistos' expedition"; "he sent Theoktistos"; "and chose flight"]

…teeth, from which a horse's age is known. But the horse was unruly and kept rearing, and this vexed the emperor, since he had no one bold enough to tame it. While he was vexed, Theophilitzes, who was present, [said], "I have a young man, very skilled and brave with horses, just such as Your Majesty is looking for. His name is Basil." The emperor ordered him to come, and a koitonites was sent to the Iron Gate. He found Basil and quickly brought him to the emperor. Basil was ordered to hold the horse. With one hand he took hold of the bridle, with the other he grasped its ear, and he turned it as gentle as a sheep. The emperor was delighted and won over, and he handed him over to Andrew the hetaeriarch to be enrolled in the Hetaireia and to serve among his horses.

I have thought it necessary to tell about this Basil, his upbringing and where he came from. He was born in Macedonia, in the villages around Adrianople, in the reign of Michael Rangabe, the father of Ignatius the patriarch. In Michael's reign Krum, the ruler of Bulgaria, marched against the Christians. Michael was routed, and Leo the Armenian rebelled against him and became emperor. Krum came and surrounded the City, but he was wounded by a spear thrust by Leo the Armenian. As he returned to Bulgaria he sent to St Mamas and carried off the bronze animal statues there. He also went to Adrianople, took it, and deported twelve thousand men, not counting women, settling them as far as the Danube.

In the days of the emperor Theophilus there was a general in Macedonia called Kordyles. He had a son named Bardas, fully grown, whom he left in his place to govern the Macedonians beyond the river Danube. He himself, by some stratagem, made his way to Theophilus, who received him gladly. Learning what he wanted, the emperor sent ships to pick them up and bring them to the City. The ruler of Bulgaria at that time was Vladimir, the grandson of Krum and father of Symeon. The people resolved to go off to Romania with their wives and children. While Michael the Bulgarian was away at Thessalonica, they began to cross with their possessions. When the Kames [Krum] learned this, he crossed over to fight them. The Macedonians, in desperation, made Tzantzes and Kordyles their leaders, and when they joined battle they killed many, and some

they took prisoner. The Bulgarians who were unable to cross streamed off to the Hungarians and told them everything about the Macedonians. The emperor's ships also arrived to pick them up and bring them to the City. At once Huns appeared, past counting. When the Macedonians saw them they cried out in tears, saying, "God of Saint Adrian, help us!" And they drew up for battle. The Turks said to them, "Give us all your property and go wherever you like." They refused, and stayed in battle order for three days. On the fourth day they began to board their ships. Seeing this, the Turks attacked, fighting from the fifth hour until evening. The nation was routed, and the Macedonians pursued them. The next day, as they were preparing to withdraw, the Huns appeared again to fight them. Then another of the Macedonians rose up, named Leo, of the family of [?], who later became hetaeriarch, along with other renowned Macedonians [?], and they drove them off. Then they turned back, boarded the ships, and came safely to the emperor. He rewarded them, and they returned to Macedonia, their own country.

Basil was then a youth who had come back from captivity. He had spent his captivity under the emperor Leo and Michael the Amorian, and came out [under Theo]philus the emperor, so that he was twenty-five years old [?]. After he had been restored to his own country, [? garbled] … called Tzantzes. When he got no help from him, [he came] as far as the Golden Gate. Having entered, worn out from the journey (for it was Sunday and the sun was setting), he lay down on the bench of St Diomedes. For the church was then a parish church, and it had a custodian named [Nicho]las. That night a divine voice called the custodian, saying, "Get up and bring the emperor into the house of prayer." He got up but found no one except Basil himself lying there like a pauper. So he turned back, shut the gate and lay down again. And at once someone struck him in the side with a sword, saying, "Go out and bring in the man you see lying outside the gate. He is the emperor." So he hurried out, trembling, and finding Basil with his bag and his staff he brought him into the church. The next day he took him to the bath and gave him a change of clothes. Coming back to the church, he made a pact of brotherhood with him, and they [?] each other.

This Nicholas had a brother, a physician, who was in the service of [Theophilitzes]. The physician happened to come to his brother, and when he saw Basil, he marvelled at his size and strength and said to his brother, "Where is this man from?" He [said] [?] … he longed for the abundance of the great city; and so, having arrived [?] …

…he told him everything and charged him to keep the secret. The physician was sitting at table with Theophilitzes, and his master, thinking aloud, said, "I cannot find a suitable man for the horses." The physician rose and told his master about Basil's strength, saying that he was just the sort of man he was looking for. So Theophilitzes sent for him at once and brought him in. Seeing that he was a young man with a big head, he gave him the nickname Kephalas and put him to work with the horses. As was said before, this is how he came to give him to the emperor Michael. So much for Basil's upbringing.

The emperor brought this Basil in and said joyfully to his mother, "Come and see, mother, what a young man I have just taken on." She came out, looked at him, and turned away, saying to her son, "This, my child, is the one who will destroy our family." But he would not be persuaded by his own mother's words, nor did he listen to her.

The patriarch Methodios, now among the saints, died, and in his place Ignatius, the son of Michael the kouropalates, was ordained.

As the Bulgarians were making raids into Thrace and Macedonia and plundering the [western?] themes, Theodora organized an expedition. Men attacking from the [?] of Bulgaria here and there, raiding in small bands, killed them and took them captive, so that the Bulgarians were held down in their own land.

Bardas the Caesar made friends with Damian, the patrician and parakoimomenos. Damian [persuaded] the emperor [to allow] Bardas to enter the City. Bardas won over the emperor's intimates with gifts and, together with the parakoimomenos, was given leave to come to the palace. He also won over Theophanes the protospatharios, surnamed Phalganos, as a man of courage, [and plotted] to kill Theoktistos the kanikleios. The emperor too was persuaded by Damian and agreed that this should be done, for Bardas kept saying to Damian, "As long as Theoktistos is with the Augusta, the emperor will neither rule nor [?]." Theoktistos went, as was his custom, to the [?] of Arabindos [?], and then, holding the petitions, he entered the Lausiakos. Looking around, he saw Bardas sitting [?]. Greatly disturbed, he said, "I [?] to the Augusta [?]." As he went into the [?], Michael and Damian met him and would not let him [go on to the Augusta?], but he was ordered [?] [the rest of the paragraph is garbled]

…in anger to open the petitions and read them out in front of them. When he had done so, unwillingly, the emperor sent him back out the way he had come. He went out weeping bitterly and lamenting. Bardas met him at the Lausiakos and began to strike him on the temple and pull out his hair. Seeing this, Maniakes, the droungarios of the Watch, stood up and protested to Bardas that he should not beat the logothete. Bardas answered that he was doing it at the emperor's command. Then the emperor himself appeared, as Damian had planned. When Bardas saw him, he and Theophanes Phalganos seized the logothete, slaughtered him, and hacked him limb from limb at the Skyla.

Theodora learned of this from the papias. She came out to confront Michael and, as was natural, was furious. Although the emperor tried in every way to appease his mother, she remained inconsolable, neither letting go of her anger nor allowing anyone to comfort her. So the emperor changed, in his demeanour and conduct as much as in his heart and mind, and set about grieving her in as many ways as he had earlier pretended to please her. He drove his sisters Thekla, Anastasia and Anna out of the palace and brought them down to the Karianos. Pulcheria, as their mother's favourite, he sent to the monastery of Gastria. Then, a little later, he brought them all together in the monastery of Gastria and had them tonsured. Acclaimed by the whole senate, he ruled alone, and he promoted Bardas magistros and domestic of the Schools.

Since his mother would not be reconciled, there was implacable enmity between them. He brought her down to the monastery called Ta Gastria and sent her there. Her mind agitated by despondency, she devised a plot against Bardas unworthy of herself. Along with many others, she sought to make the emperor's protostrator an accomplice, so that they might kill Bardas as he was returning from his suburban estate. But their scheme came to light before it was carried out, and the evil they had plotted fell on the plotters themselves. They were detected and arrested, and were beheaded at the Sphendone. And Michael promoted Basil protostrator in place of the dead man, and likewise promoted his uncle Bardas kouropalates.

At that time dust fell from the sky onto the roof tiles, blood-like and in great quantity, and many people found stones in the streets or in gardens as red as blood.

Michael promoted Antigonos, Bardas' son, domestic of the Schools. To his other son he gave a wife, with whom he was also reviled [?], and promoted him monostrategos over

He brought his magnates into the city and baptized them all, and from then on there was deep peace. When Amer marched out against Romania again, Petronas, who was general of the East, and Nasr of the Boukellarioi lay in ambush on his road home and met him at Lalakaon. Battle was joined and they routed Amer. As he fled, one of the counts pursued him, cut off his head and brought it to the general Petronas. The generals entered the city in victory and celebrated a triumph over them in the Hippodrome. From then on there was great calm in the East because of the slaughter of Amer. And the labours of others, and the brave deeds against the enemy... [?] But the emperor's love was poured out on Basil, and he thought him the only one who truly served him. Michael built a stable for his horses, adorning it with marbles and fitting it with running water, and made it very beautiful. When it was finished, there was a man in the city named Peter, learned and fond of mockery, whom people also called the Beggar-Magister. Michael summoned him to the stable and showed him the splendour of this house for dumb beasts, wanting to be praised by him; and he said [?] that he would be remembered forever for building this work. But Peter said to the emperor: "Justinian built the Great Church and adorned it with gold and silver and precious marbles, and now there is no memory of him. And you, emperor, who have made a dung-heap and a resting place for beasts, say you will be remembered for this?" Michael, failing to get praise from him and growing angry, had the Beggar-Magister beaten and dragged out. When a rumour spread about the Caesar Bardas that he was having illicit relations with his daughter-in-law, the patriarch Ignatius heard of it and often urged him to keep away from such defilement and not to be a stumbling block to many, since he ought to be a model of virtue and of a temperate life. But Bardas would not listen and bore a grudge against the patriarch. And once, when Bardas was about to receive communion, the patriarch turned him away, not without reason or cause [?], as one

who would not obey canons or admonitions. Bardas, stung to the soul with anger, drove out his admonisher as a lawless man and a corrupter of the Church, and subjected him to countless savage tortures to force him to resign. When Ignatius would not yield, he had Photius ordained patriarch in his place; Photius was protoasecretis at the time and a very learned man. The emperor marched against the Hagarenes, leaving Ooryphas, the eparch, in the city to guard it. The emperor had not yet gone far, nor accomplished anything at all of what he had in mind, when Ooryphas sent word of the arrival of the godless Rus, who had already reached the Black River. So the emperor broke off the journey he was on, accomplished nothing of what he had set out for, and did nothing kingly or noble. The Rus got inside the Hieron, wrought great slaughter among the Christians and shed innocent blood. There were two hundred ships, which surrounded the city and struck great fear into those within. The emperor arrived and with difficulty managed to cross over, and with the patriarch Photius he went to the church of the Mother of God at Blachernae, and there they sought to appease God. Then, singing hymns, they brought out the holy veil of the Theotokos and dipped its hem in the sea. Though there was a calm, at once winds sprang up, and the sea, which had been still, rose in wave upon wave; the ships of the godless Rus were shattered, and only a few escaped the danger. Once, as the Caesar Bardas was passing in procession to the Horologion wearing a scarlet scaramangion, the patrician and parakoimomenos Damian, who was sitting there, did not rise to do him honour. Seeing this, the Caesar was furious; he went into the Chrysotriklinos and sat down with the emperor, weeping with anger and rage, and the emperor asked the reason. He said: "By the command of your majesty I was granted great honour, but Damian, to the reproach of you and of your majesty, did not rise before [?] the senate." The emperor was angered and at once ordered a certain Maximian, a koitonites, to seize Damian and take him off to the harbour of Saint Mamas, first to tonsure him and then to keep him under guard; and that same day he promoted Basil the protostrator to parakoimomenos. When the Caesar heard this he grew jealous, and from then on he sought to kill Basil. Michael separated Basil from his own wife Maria and gave him Eudokia Ingerina as wife, ordering him to keep her as his lady.

For she was the emperor's concubine, and he loved her dearly for her beauty. To Maria, Basil's former wife, he gave gold and other things and sent her off to Macedonia to her own [?]. And he assigned his own sister Thekla to Basil, for him to keep privately. From then on the Caesar and Basil eyed each other with suspicion, each seeking how to destroy the other. Basil privately slandered the Caesar as plotting against the emperor. Eager to convince the emperor, Basil made friends with Symbatios, patrician and logothete of the drome, who was the Caesar's son-in-law, and they bound themselves by oaths to be in harmony and lasting friendship. Basil also assured Symbatios with dreadful oaths: "The emperor has great love for you, and I am pressing your cause; he plans to promote you to Caesar, but because of your father-in-law he cannot do it." Deceived by Basil's oaths, Symbatios turned against the Caesar Bardas, his own father-in-law. He went in to the emperor and swore to him, assuring him, "The Caesar wants to kill you," and disclosed the details of the plot. The emperor, persuaded by Symbatios's oaths and confirmed in it by Basil's words, nursed resentment against the Caesar. Basil, knowing that everything had been well arranged against the Caesar but that he could not carry it out in the city, persuaded the emperor to set a fleet and army in motion against Crete. When this happened, Leo the Philosopher advised the Caesar Bardas to be on his guard and to protect himself from Basil. The Caesar, in turn, urged the emperor to keep clear of Basil. When the procession to the Chalkoprateia for the Annunciation took place, after the entrance had been made and the Gospel read, the patriarch [?] and the emperor, with the Caesar and Basil the parakoimomenos, went up to the galleries, the [?] holding in his hands the precious body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. The emperor and Basil, dipping their pens in it, signed the precious crosses, confirming by oath that the Caesar could go out with them on the campaign without fear. For Leo the Philosopher had openly urged Bardas not to go with them, saying that if he went out he would not return. After the feast of holy [?], the emperor set out with a great army and reached the theme of the Thrakesians. When they had encamped at Kepoi, Basil the parakoimomenos laid a plan to kill the Caesar. In the plot were his brother Marianos, Peter the Bulgarian, John of Chaldia, and Constantine

Toxaras. But John the Neatokomes found out about it. He went down to the Caesar's tent at sunset, met Prokopios, the Caesar's protovestiarios, and assured him: "Tomorrow your master the Caesar will be cut to pieces." Prokopios went in and reported this to the Caesar. On hearing it the Caesar said to Prokopios: "Go and tell the Neatokomes: 'It is you who are sowing these tares.'" At early dawn he summoned all his people, explained to them what he had been told, and asked their advice. Philotheos, protospatharios and genikos, who was dear to him, said to the Caesar: "Tomorrow, master, put on your gold-and-purple tunic and show yourself to your enemies, and they will flee before your face." At sunrise he mounted his horse and came to the emperor's tent in splendid dress. Constantine Toxaras, by Basil's plan, went out to meet him and did him obeisance, and informed Basil of his arrival. Basil came out, did him obeisance, took him by the hand and led him to the emperor. The Caesar sat down beside the emperor and said: "Now that the whole army is assembled, master, give the order to cross over to Crete." Basil, standing behind him, struck him with his sword, and the others after him cut him to pieces while the emperor looked on; it was the third hour of the day. The emperor and Basil at once returned to the city. As they were coming past the market of Akritas, where a great crowd had gathered to see the emperor, a man dressed in monastic habit cried out to the emperor from a high rock: "A fine campaign you have made, emperor, killing your own kinsman, your own father's blood, with the sword! Woe to you, woe to you, for doing this!" The emperor and Basil, enraged, sent the manglabites Maurotheodore to kill the monk with the sword. But the people ran up and said he was mad and possessed, and so he barely escaped punishment. Late on the Saturday of Pentecost the emperor sent word to the patriarch Photius, through Rentakios his protovestiarios, to carry out the proclamation of Basil as emperor; and the next day two thrones were brought out. The people were troubled at how, when there was one emperor, two thrones had been brought out. As the emperor passed in procession, Basil walked behind him wearing a scaramangion and carrying a sword, as is the custom for parakoimomenoi. When the emperor reached the imperial gates, he did not take off his crown, as is the custom for emperors, but went in wearing it as far as the holy doors; then, turning around, he went up three steps of the ambo with the crown on. Below the ambo stood Basil the parakoimomenos, and below Basil, Leo Kastor [the quaestor] and asecretis, holding a document in his hands, and Michael the praepositus, Ang- (59) "The gold-and-purple tunic" [?]

-oures, and the demarchs together with the demes. Then Leo the asecretis began to read, saying: "Bardas the Caesar plotted against me to kill me, and for this reason he led me out of the city; and had it not been revealed to me by Symbatios and Basil, I would not be among the living. He has died through his own sin. It is my wish that Basil the parakoimomenos, as one who is faithful, who guards my reign and has freed me from my enemy, should be guardian of my reign and be acclaimed by all as emperor." Basil was filled with tears. The emperor took the crown from his own head and gave it to the patriarch Photius to carry in to the holy table, and he himself said a prayer over it; and the praepositi brought the divetesion and the tzangia and clothed Basil, who, putting on the chlamys, fell at the emperor's feet. Then the patriarch came out and took up [the crown] [?] and handed it to the emperor; and when the sceptres had been lowered, as is customary, Michael crowned Basil, and all acclaimed: "Many years to Michael and Basil!" Kastor the asecretis, who had read out the document, went off to Nicomedia, came to a monastery of men and stayed in the middle of the meadow. There was a well there; he fell into it and drowned, and was buried there. Symbatios, the Caesar's son-in-law, having failed to obtain the rank of Caesar and seeing that he had been made a fool of by Basil, was moved to hatred against Basil. He took counsel with George Peganes, the general, and the next day asked to be appointed a strategos instead of [his present office]. Goumer was appointed logothete of the drome in his place, while Peganes was count of the Opsikion. Symbatios and Peganes went out together and began to ravage and burn the countryside and the vineyards (for it was summer), acclaiming Michael alone and execrating Basil. When the emperors learned of this they ordered the other generals to make war on them. Nikephoros [?] devised a plan and had a written message thrown among all the people, so that they might seize them by guile and not fall into civil war by fighting openly. Peganes was captured; they brought him into the city, and by the emperor's order Constantine Mylares [?], the eparch, blinded him. They seated him at the Milion and put a bowl in his hands, and all who passed by tossed into it whatever they chose. Thirty days later Symbatios the Armenian was captured by Maleinos at an inn in Keltzene, and Maleinos brought him to the emperor, who was at Saint Mamas. By the emperor's order they brought Peganes out to meet Symbatios, putting into the hands

of Peganes an earthenware censer with which to cense him. They blinded Symbatios in one eye and cut off his right hand, and seated him at the Lausos, and put a bowl in his lap so that whoever wished might toss something into it. Three days later they took them away to their own houses and kept them under guard. The emperor Michael sent an engineer called Labaris [?] and had Constantine Kaballinos taken out of his tomb; he found the body intact, and wanting to bring it in in a sack, when it would not fit, he broke it [?]. Likewise he had the patriarch Iannes taken out of his tomb together with his omophorion. By the emperor's order the eparch shut them up in the praetorium, and on the day of the races he brought them out, stripped them and beat them with clubs, and sent their bones off and burned them at the Amastrianon. The sarcophagus of Copronymus, which was green and wonderful, he had sawn up and made into parapets for the church he had built in the palace at the Pharos. The emperor Leo was born of Michael and Eudokia Ingerina while Michael himself was still alive, on the first of the fourth month, in the fifteenth indiction. The emperor held races at Saint Mamas, himself driving for the Blues. Constantine the Armenian, father of the patrician Thomas and of Genesios, who was droungarios of the Watch, drove for the Whites; Agallianos drove for the Greens, and Krasas for the Reds. The emperor won, and when he sat down to dinner with Basil and [?], the patrician Basiliskianos praised the emperor for driving the chariot so skilfully. The emperor ordered him to stand up, and told him to pull off the emperor's red boots and put them on himself. He refused and looked at Basil, and the emperor angrily ordered him to do it. When Basil nodded to him, he put on the boots. The emperor then said to Basil with an oath: "They suit him better than you. Have I not the power, as I made you emperor, to make another one too?" And he grew angry and raged against Basil. Eudokia said to the emperor in tears: "The dignity of empire, my lord, is a great thing; we too have been honoured with it beyond our worth, and it is not right for it to be held in contempt." The emperor said: "Don't be upset about this; I mean to make Basiliskianos emperor too." Basil was filled with anger and great grief. When the emperor went out hunting, a monk met him and gave him a paper revealing the plot that Basil was devising against him. He read it and, in his anger, began plotting against Basil. When his mother Theodora invited the emperor to the Anthemiou palace, he sent Rentakios his protovestiarios with other men of his household to catch some game and send it to his mother. Basil, [?] of the fourth month [?]

was making his preparations against Michael, and was very gloomy. When the emperor sat down to dinner, he invited Eudokia and Basil as well to dine with him. When the emperor had drunk a great deal of wine, Basil got up as if for some need and went into the bedchamber, and, being strong, he bent the bolts so that the door could not be locked. Then he went back and dined again with the emperor. When the emperor was thoroughly drunk and Ingerina, as was her custom, had taken her leave of him, Michael rose and, led by the hand by Basil, went into the bedchamber; Basil kissed his hand and went out. Inside the bedchamber was Basiliskianos, sleeping on Rentakios's bed by the emperor's command, to guard him. Ignatios the koitonites went to lock the door of the bedchamber, found the bolt bent, and in despair sat down on the bed tearing his hair. While the emperor slept a sleep like death, Basil suddenly arrived with others and opened the doors. Ignatios came out in terror and struggled with Basil to keep him from going in. Peter the Bulgarian, slipping under Basil's arm, made for the emperor's bed but was grabbed by Ignatios; while they struggled, the emperor woke up. John the Chaldian at once struck at him with his sword and cut off his hands. Iakobitzes and the Persian wounded Basiliskianos with a sword and threw him down from above. Marianos, Bardas the father of Basil, and Constantine Toxaras stood outside on guard; and none of Michael's people knew what was happening. Basil's men gathered together and said: "Even if we cut off his hands, we have left him alive. If he lives, what defence shall we make?" To please Basil, the Chaldian went back and found Michael without hands, lying on the bed and lamenting against Basil. He pitilessly drove the naked sword into the emperor's heart, ripping open his entrails, and turning back he boasted to Basil as though he had done a brave deed. Though there was a storm at sea, they gathered and went down to the ferry, and crossing over they came to the house of Eulogios the Persian; taking him with them they came to the Marina quarter, and climbing over the wall they reached the palace. [?] they surround the wall, and Basil, holding on to two of his companions, kicked and broke the slab and went in as far as the palace gate. Eulogios the Persian told Artabasdos the hetaeriarch in his own language that Michael had died by the sword, and said, "Open to the emperor." Artabasdos ran to the papias, took the keys from him by force, and opened to Basil; and once inside, Basil took the keys of the pal- (41) "Invited Eudokia": the emperor invited [?] (42) [?]

[?]…of the palace, in charge of [?]; and at dawn he made a man called Gregory, the son of Philemon, papias. He at once sent to Saint Mamas and brought Eudokia, the daughter of Inger, into the palace with great pomp. He also sent John the praepositus to remove the Dekapolitissa and take her back to her own parents. He sent Paul the koitonites as well, to bury Michael. When Paul arrived, he found him wrapped in the saddle-cloth of the right-hand horse of the team he used to drive, with his entrails hanging out. Michael's mother and sisters were there, weeping and lamenting over him. Paul took them, put them in a small boat and crossed over to the monastery of Chrysopolis, and there he laid Michael out and buried him.

Basil reigned with Michael for one year and four months, and alone for twelve years. He ordered the eparch and Marianos, the son of Petronas, to go together to the Forum and, with all the people, proclaim him sole emperor. I have thought it necessary to record also the vengeance that God brought on those who did away with Michael, and what each of them suffered at various times. Jacobitzes was hunting with the emperor at the Philopation when his sword fell. He dismounted to pick it up, but before his foot reached the ground, while the other was still caught in the stirrup, the horse took fright and dragged him off. Running through ravine and ditches, it tore him limb from limb. John the Chaldian became general in Chaldia, and when he was caught plotting against the emperor, he was impaled by Andrew the general on the emperor's orders. The emperor's cousin Asyleon was banished by the emperor to his suburban estate, the one named after the Chartophylax [?]. Because he was harsh and cruel to his own slaves, they killed him with knives one night. The emperor arrested them, cut them limb from limb and burned them at the Amastrianon. Apelates the Persian was eaten by worms and departed this life. Constantine Toxaras was cut down with swords among the Kibyrrhaiots and died. And Marianos, the emperor's brother, fell from his horse and broke his legs; his foot rotted with worms, and he died. On the day of Christ's Nativity the emperor went out in procession to the Great Church and baptized his son Stephen. Then he had white horses brought with a chariot and sat in it together with the Augusta, and the praepositus Baanes rode with them, carrying the child all the way to the palace, while the emperor scattered consular largesse along the road. On the feast of Saint Polyeuktos there was a tremendous earthquake, so that the earth shook for forty days and forty nights. At that time the sphere of the [?] of the Forum fell, and so did the Sigma of the all-holy Theotokos, killing everyone who was chanting there. Leo the Philosopher, who happened to be there,

told the chanters and everyone else present to leave the church; but they did not heed him, and they all perished. The Philosopher himself stood against a column beneath the [?] and was saved along with two others, and only five others survived, beneath the ambo. When the emperor came into the church and was about to receive communion, Patriarch Photius called him a robber and a murderer, unworthy of divine communion. In his anger the emperor sent to Rome and obtained a tome, with Roman bishops; he drove Photius from his throne and appointed Ignatius, now among the saints, patriarch for the second time. The emperor Alexander was born to him by Eudokia, the daughter of Inger. He was a child and legitimate son of Basil. The emperor campaigned against the Hagarenes of Tephrike. He joined battle and was defeated, and in his many encounters with the Hagarenes he lost many of the Romans. During this flight of the emperor, Theophylact Abastaktos, the father of Romanos who reigned later, saved the emperor when he was on the point of being captured by the Hagarenes. Afterwards the emperor sought him out and identified him (for many men were telling the emperor, "It was I"). Theophylact declined the honour and asked instead for an imperial estate, which he received. When the emperor returned to the city, he sent his brother-in-law Christopher to Tephrike; Christopher won a very great victory, sacked the town and razed it to the ground. Patriarch Ignatius built a very beautiful church at the market of Satyros, dedicated to the Archistrategos of the East [?], and founded a monastery for men there, where his body also lies. Thekla, the sister, sent a humble man of hers to the emperor with a petition, and the emperor asked him, "Who has your mistress?" He said, "Neatokometes." The emperor at once had him brought, beat him, tonsured him and put him in the monastic habit. In the same way he sent his protovestiarios Prokopios, who beat Thekla, seized all her money and brought it to the emperor. Later the emperor made Neatokometes steward of the Great Church. This same emperor baptized all the Hebrews who were under his rule at that time, with all the dignitaries acting as their sponsors; he treated them kindly and gave them gifts. As for the Nicholas Androsalites mentioned above, who was also the prosmonarios of Saint Diomedes [?] … Church, and to the children [?] the father [?] … [?]

[Running head: Chronography] [?] …to whom the martyr appeared, as was said earlier, the emperor honoured him by making him steward and synkellos. His brother John he made droungarios of the Watch; their other brother Paul, head of the Sakellion; and the fourth brother, general logothete. When Nicholas the synkellos died, they buried him at the Arkadianai in his own house, where the metochion of Saint Constantine is. The emperor received word that Syracuse was being sacked by the Hagarenes. Because the sailors were busy with the building and earthworks [?] of the New Church, Syracuse was surrendered before the emperor's fleet arrived, and he grieved greatly over it. Niketas Xylinites, the epi tes trapezes, was accused of being the lover of the Augusta, so the emperor tonsured him and made him a monk. Under Emperor Leo he became steward of the Great Church, and when he died he was laid to rest in the monastery that he himself had built, where he had also tonsured his sisters. For the New Church the emperor took a great deal of marble and many mosaic tesserae from many churches. Among these was a bronze statue that stood in the Sennaton [?], in the figure of a bishop; in its hand it held a staff with a serpent coiled round it. They took it down and put it in the vestiarion. When the emperor came down and went into the place where the statue stood upright, he put his finger to the serpent's mouth. A live snake was in there, and it bit the emperor's finger, which was barely healed with antidotes, and everyone marvelled at this. He also broke up the statue of Solomon, a very large one that stood in the Basilica, and ordered it to be recast in his own name and placed down in the foundations of the same New Church, as though offering himself as a sacrifice to this building and to God. The emperor campaigned again, against Melitene, took many captives, fought many battles and returned. Ignatius, the patriarch now among the saints, died, and in his place the emperor again raised Photius to the patriarchate. Later, when Patriarch Photius died in exile, his body was laid in the monastery called that of Eremia at Merdosagares. It had formerly been a parish church, but Photius made it a convent for women. Once more the emperor marched against Syria, to Germanikeia; he sacked it, took captives and returned. Constantine, the son of Emperor Michael by Eudokia, died, and Basil mourned him greatly. On the first of May the church that the emperor had built was enthroned and dedicated by Patriarch Photius, and it was adorned with great splendour; [?] … [Cedrenus: "Constantine, the elder of the emperor's sons, died of a fever."] [?]

…the emperor wore the loros at its dedication, gave much money and named it the New Church. [?] …and he worked marvels and had the gift of foresight. Photius recommended him to Emperor Basil and presented him [?] … it, of Saint Constantine [?]. By these and very many other such things, as one thoroughly versed in the works of Apollonius [?], the man called Santabarenos made the emperor put great trust in him. The emperor took as a wife for Emperor Leo the daughter of Martinakios, and he crowned her as well, holding the wedding in the Magnaura and in the Nineteen Couches. Emperor Leo was denounced to his father by Santabarenos: "He carries a dagger, intending to kill you with it." It was Santabarenos himself who had advised Leo to have this very dagger made and to carry it in his boot. He had told him, "Your father often asks for a knife for some need or other; why do you not [?]…?" Leo had it made. Then Santabarenos slandered him, and he was caught carrying it in his boot. He pleaded his case at length but did not [?]. So his protovestiarios Niketas, who later became [?] under Emperor Romanos, was beaten, and others with him suffered many terrible things and were sent into exile. The emperor shut Leo up in the Pearl chamber and [?] to blind him, had not the patriarch [?] … [?]

…with many entreaties he prevented this, together with Zaoutzes [?] Stylianos, the minor hetaireiarch. Leo spent three months out of the emperor's sight, weeping and lamenting, and he sent many letters imploring the emperor. Since the emperor had great faith in Saint Elijah, Emperor Leo was restored to his presence on the commemoration of Saint Elijah. When the procession took place, the people saw him and cried out, "Glory to you, O God!" The emperor turned round and answered them: "Do you glorify God for my son? You will have to endure many afflictions from him, and painful days." Andrew, the domestic of the Schools, was accused by Santabarenos before the emperor of siding with Leo, and the emperor removed him. In his place Stoupiotes was appointed domestic. He went with an army to Tarsus and was defeated, and the emperor appointed Andrew domestic again. A conspiracy against the emperor was formed by John Kourkouas, the domestic of the Hikanatoi, after he received an oracle from a recluse at Blachernae. Many senators and other officials were found to be involved with him, as many as sixty-six. Among them were Michael the hetaireiarch, Katoudares, Myxares, Baboutzikos and the rest. When the plot was revealed to the emperor by the protovestiarios of Kourkouas [?] ….. When they had all been brought down, the emperor went out to the Hippodrome and sat there. He examined their case, had them all beaten and shaved, and burned whatever hair was left. After this he went out in the procession of the Annunciation, the occasion on which they had intended to carry out the plot. On his orders they walked before him, naked and bound, as far as the Forum. Then he confiscated all their property and exiled them. Once, when the emperor went out hunting, a huge stag appeared from somewhere. As the emperor was chasing it, it turned and caught him by the belt with its antler, lifting him off his horse. Someone [?] drew his sword, cut through the belt and rescued the emperor. After he got back, the emperor ordered that the man who had cut the belt be beheaded, for having drawn his sword against him. The man pleaded at length, "I did this for your sake," but it did him no good. From the [?] … [?] … to be restored to his presence

…Basil fell ill from the stag's mauling and died, leaving Leo as emperor, and Alexander. LEO. Leo, the son of Basil, reigned for twenty-five years and eight months. His brother Stephen was synkellos; he had been raised and educated by Patriarch Photius. When Emperor Leo became sole ruler, he sent Andrew the general to Chrysopolis with many candles, clergy and senators. They took Michael out of his tomb and placed him in a coffin of cypress wood. They set him on a bier, covered him in imperial fashion and honoured him with hymns and great ceremony, while his brothers also followed, and they brought him to the Holy Apostles and laid him in a sarcophagus. After this the emperor sent Andrew, the domestic of the Schools, together with John Hagiopolites, a most learned man who had been logothete of the Drome. They went up into the ambo of the church, read out the charges against Patriarch Photius and deposed him from his throne. Then they took him up to the monastery of the Armenians, the one called [?]. The emperor appointed Stylianos Zaoutzes magistros and logothete of the Drome. He brought his brother Stephen up to the patriarchate, and before Christmas Stephen was ordained patriarch by Theophanes the protothronos and the other archbishops. He held the patriarchate for six years and five months, and when he died he was buried in the monastery [?]. In Leo's reign the fortress called Hypsele was betrayed and taken by the Hagarenes, and everyone there was taken captive. There was also a great fire near the Sophiai, and the church of the holy apostle Thomas burned too; Leo himself restored it splendidly. The emperor sent to Euchaita and brought Theodore Santabarenos to the city. Andrew the domestic and Stephen the magistros, the son of Kalomaria, who had both been badly slandered by Santabarenos, concocted a plot and suggested to the emperor that Patriarch Photius and Theodore Santabarenos had planned to make one of Patriarch Photius's own kin emperor. The emperor ordered Patriarch Photius and Theodore Santabarenos to be brought to the palace of Pege, and directed that they be guarded separately. The emperor sent Stephen the magistros, Andrew the domestic, the patricians Krateros and Gouber, and John Hagiopolites to examine (58) Supply: "being a cleric, he was also synkellos." So [?]. Supply: "being a cleric, he was also synkellos." So [?].

the charges against them (60). They brought in the patriarch and seated him on a throne with honour, and when they had taken their own seats, Andrew the domestic said to the patriarch, "Do you know Abba Theodore, master?" He replied, "I do not know any Abba Theodore." Andrew said, "You do not know Abba Theodore Santabarenos?" The patriarch answered, "I know Abba Theodore, who is archbishop of Euchaita." Then they brought in Santabarenos too, and Andrew the domestic said to him, "The emperor sends you this message: 'Where are the money and the property of my imperial office?'" He replied, "They are wherever the emperor of the day gave them. Now that he orders them to be searched for, he has the authority to take them." Andrew said to him, "Tell me: whom did you want to make emperor, when by your scheming you urged my father to blind me? A kinsman of the patriarch, or one of your own?" He answered, "I know nothing at all about this." Then Stephen the magistros said, "Then how did you send word to the emperor that you would convict the patriarch on this?" At once Santabarenos fell at the patriarch's feet and said, "I adjure you by God, my master, first to depose me; then, once I am stripped of the priesthood, let them punish me as a criminal. For I never told the emperor any such thing." Before them all the patriarch said, "By the salvation of my soul, lord Theodore, you are archbishop both in this present age and in the age to come." At this Andrew grew angry and said, "Abba, did you not send word to the emperor through me, saying, 'I will convict the patriarch on this'?" But he denied knowing anything. So they went back and reported to the emperor what had been said. Seized by uncontrollable fury and rage at having found no charge against the patriarch, the emperor sent men who beat Santabarenos severely and exiled him to Athens. Then he sent [?] again, had him blinded and exiled him to the East. Many years later the emperor gave in to entreaties, brought him back into the city and ordered that he receive provisions from the New Church. Santabarenos died in the time of Constantine and his mother Zoe. During Leo's reign Aion the Lombard, a duke who had become son-in-law of the [?] of Francia, rebelled against the emperor and brought the whole country under his control. When the emperor learned of this, he sent Constantine the epi tes trapezes with all the themes of the West to make war on Aion. In the battle Constantine's men were defeated and slaughtered, and he himself barely escaped. There was an eclipse of the sun, (60) Continuator: "examiners of the charges against them." (62) "You are archbishop, both in the present…": as also [?] … [?]

so that it was night for six hours and the stars could be seen. There was thunder too, with gathering winds and lightning, so that seven people were burned to death on the steps of the Forum. The fortress of Samos was besieged by the Hagarenes, and the general, Paspalas, was taken captive. Emperor Leo appointed Zaoutzes basileopator, having already become intimate with his daughter Zoe after her husband, Theodore Gouzouniates, died of some poison. When Patriarch Stephen departed this life, Antony, called Kauleas, was ordained in his place. News came from the general of Macedonia that Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, meant to march against Romania. The cause of Symeon's anger was this. Zaoutzes the basileopator had a eunuch slave named Mousikos. He became friends with Stauracius and Cosmas, men from Hellas who loved gold and were merchants. With an eye to shameful gain, and through the [?] and influence of Mousikos, they moved the Bulgarians' market from the city to Thessalonica, and treated the Bulgarians badly in collecting the customs duties. The Bulgarians reported this to Symeon, and he informed Emperor Leo. But the emperor was held back by the basileopator, who favoured Mousikos, and he dismissed the whole matter as nonsense. So the Bulgarian flew into a rage and marched against the Romans. When the emperor learned of this, he sent Krenites the general against the Bulgarians with weapons and many officials of the city. Battle was joined in Macedonia and the Romans were routed: Krenites was killed, along with Kourtikios the Armenian and all the rest. Symeon captured some of the Khazars who served in Leo's hetaireia, cut off their noses and sent them back to the city, to the shame of the Romans. When the emperor saw them he was enraged, and he sent Niketas, called Skleros, with dromons to the river Danube to give gifts to the Turks and stir them to war against Symeon. He went and met their chiefs, Arpad and Kousan; they agreed to fight, and he took hostages and came back to the emperor. The emperor again sent the patrician Eustathios, droungarios of the fleet, by sea, and sent the patrician Nikephoros Phokas, the domestic, by land with the themes, and he advanced as far as Bulgaria. Since the emperor welcomed peace, he afterwards also sent Constantinakios the quaestor to Symeon to urge a peace settlement. But Symeon, seeing the forces moving against him by both land and sea, put the quaestor under guard, claiming he had come with deceitful intent. Crossing over [?]…

[?] ...while Symeon was busy with Phokas's army, the Turks carried off all Bulgaria into captivity. When Symeon learned of this, he moved against the Turks. They crossed over and joined battle with the Bulgarians, and Symeon was routed and barely escaped to safety in Dristra. The Turks then asked the emperor to send men to buy the Bulgarian captives, and the emperor did so, sending the citizens [?] to buy them. Symeon, through Eustathios the drungarios, sued for peace, and the emperor agreed. He sent Leo Choirosphaktes to make peace. Nikephoros (67) received orders to return with the army, and so did the drungarios Eustathios. But Symeon did not think Leo worth even a word, and shut him up in prison. Then Symeon marched against the Turks, who had no stronghold [?] and no help from the Romans but had been left unprovided for, and slaughtered them all. With his pride swollen by this, he returned and found Leo at Moundraga, and said to him: "I will not make peace unless I receive all the captives." So the emperor ordered them to be handed back. Theodore the Bulgarian, a confidant of Symeon, came with Leo and took charge of them. After Nikephoros Phokas died, Symeon looked for pretexts to break the peace, and he came against the Romans demanding other captives. Emperor Leo appointed Leo Katakalon, who lived in Rhaidestos, as domestic of the scholai. He sent the patrician and protovestiarios Theodosios with him, along with [?] all the themes and the tagmata. When battle was joined with Symeon at Bulgarophygon, there was a general rout and everyone perished, including the patrician Theodosios, whose loss grieved the emperor deeply. At this time the men of the kapros [?] in Cherson also murdered their strategos, Symeon son of Jonas, and the Hagarenes took the fortress of Koron in Cappadocia. The emperor made an excursion to Ta Damianou, accompanied by Zaoutzes, who shared his power (68), and by Zaoutzes' daughter Zoe. His wife Theophano was not there; she was persevering in prayer at the Holy Soros in Blachernai.
