When the emperor decided to stay there, the kinsmen of Zaoutzes, his son Tzantzes and the others, held a council and planned to kill the emperor during the night. Zoe was sleeping with the emperor and heard the commotion. She looked out at them through the window and kept quiet [?], but when she realized what a terrible plot they had devised, she woke the emperor. He immediately boarded a ship and crossed to Pegai, leaving Zaoutzes and all the others there. Early in the morning he went quickly into the palace and removed John, drungarios... He had Zoe, the daughter of [?] [Zaoutzes], with him, and Zaoutzes himself.

...of the Watch, and appointed Pardos (69), son of Nicholas, his hetaireiarch. This Nicholas had become friendly with the emperor and was revealing all of Zaoutzes' affairs to him. From then on the emperor did not go [?] to Zaoutzes' chamber, until the magistros Leo and Theodotakes reconciled them. The Augusta Theophano died after reigning twelve years. Not many days later God showed her to be a wonder-worker, because she had been free of jealousy and resentment and had persevered without ceasing in almsgiving and prayer to God and in the holy churches. Emperor Leo then crowned Zoe, the daughter of Zaoutzes, and was married to her by a palace cleric nicknamed Sinapes. The man who performed the wedding was deposed (71). She reigned one year and eight months. When this Zoe died, a sarcophagus was found in the [?] for her body, with letters carved inside that read: "Daughter of Babylon, the wretched." Leo Mousikos (72) and Staurakios were denounced to the emperor for taking gifts from the strategos and the officials (73) and acting as their go-betweens with the basileopator. Once Staurakios came in with a letter for Zaoutzes. When the emperor saw him standing in the heliakon, he came up behind him, took him by the scruff of the neck and led him outside, as though to ask him about the strategos (74). He brought him to the Monothyron, took the letters and flung them away, and handed him over to the bystanders to put him out of the palace, with orders that he be tonsured. When Mousikos learned of this, he fell into despair. The emperor then went in where Mousikos was standing in attendance on Zaoutzes, shoved him out by the neck, and handed him over to Christopher the koitonites to take him to the Stoudios monastery and make him a monk. Shortly afterwards Zaoutzes died in the palace. They carried him down through the Boukoleon and took him to the monastery of Kauleas to bury him there. After Zaoutzes' death Basil Epeiktes, son of Nicholas the hetaireiarch, made friends with the koubikoularios Samonas, the man of Hagarene descent, because he was aiming at imperial rank. He confided in Samonas: "Now that our aunt Zoe is dead, the emperor is going to take another wife and wants to destroy us all. But give me your word, and I will confide to you everything that is being planned." When Samonas gave Basil his word, Basil confided everything to him. Samonas went in to the emperor and said to him: "My lord, I want to tell you something in private. If I tell it, I die; if I do not tell it, you die." [Notes: (72) "To Emperor Leo, Mousikos." Thus correctly. (73) "from the strategoi and officials"; which [?] (74) "to ask about the strategoi", as if [?]]

[Chronographia] And he laid out (75) to the emperor the whole of Basil's plot. The emperor did not believe what he said, and replied: "Didn't someone put you up to telling me this? Didn't you do it for a bribe?" He answered: "Send trustworthy men of your choosing into my cell, my lord, so that they can hide there, and let them write down whatever they hear from Basil and from me." At once the emperor sent the protovestiarios Christopher together with the koitonites Kalokyros, and they went in and hid in Samonas's cell. Basil, taking the bait, received a sworn pledge from Samonas in his oratory and told him everything about the plot and who the conspirators were. When the two of them got up (76), Christopher and Kalokyros came down and read everything out to the emperor. The emperor immediately summoned Basil and gave him twenty thousand miliaresia (77), supposedly set aside for the soul of his aunt Zoe, and sent him to Macedonia. In this way he got Basil out of the city. As for the others who had taken part in his plot, he sent Pardos, drungarios of the Watch, to Stypiotes, supposedly to fetch him, but had instructed Pardos beforehand by imperial note (78) to arrest him. Then the emperor, on the pretext of going to dine at St Lazarus at the descent [?] of the Tzykanisterion (79), stationed John Garidas with the rest of the hetaireia in the koubouklion. As the emperor was coming down, Nicholas the hetaireiarch was seized along with John, and he was expelled from the city. The emperor brought Basil back from Macedonia, interrogated him, had him flogged, had his hair burned off, paraded him through the Mese, and exiled him to Athens, where he died miserably. Likewise Nicholas the hetaireiarch, Stylianos, John and the whole family of Zaoutzes: some he tonsured, others he exiled, and he confiscated their property. Then the emperor summoned all the magistroi and the high officials and read out before them what Samonas had disclosed. They praised Samonas lavishly for having looked after the emperor's life, and said he deserved the highest honour. At once the emperor honoured him with the rank of protospatharios. The patriarch Stephen died, and in his place Nicholas, the emperor's mystikos (80), was ordained patriarch. The fortress of Demetrias in the theme of Hellas was taken by Damian the Hagarene. Emperor Leo crowned Anna, his daughter by Zoe the daughter of Zaoutzes, because the customary banquets could not be held without an Augusta. The emperor took as his wife a very beautiful girl from the theme of Opsi- [Notes: (75) Anonymous: "went through". (76) "When they got up" [?] Anonymous [?]. (77) Anonymous: "twenty-four thousand". Edition [?] "through Basiliskos Pittakios" [?], by [?]]

-kion, named Eudokia. He crowned her, had her proclaimed, and married her. She bore him a male child, but she died in giving birth, and so did the child. The emperor bought houses near the Holy Apostles and built a very beautiful church dedicated to his first wife, Saint Theophano. He also built St Lazarus at the place called Ta Topou, founding there a monastery for eunuch men. He deposited there the body of Saint Lazarus and of Mary Magdalene [?] (81), and held the dedication of the church. [?] of these churches, Taormina in Sicily was taken by the Africans through the negligence, or rather the treachery, of Eustathios, drungarios of the fleet, of Karamalos, who was there, and of Michael Charaktos, and the Romans were slaughtered in great numbers. When they came up to the city, Michael Charaktos accused them before the emperor and the patriarch of being traitors, and they were condemned to death. But Patriarch Nicholas pleaded with the emperor, and they were spared death. They were only flogged, had their property confiscated, and were tonsured as monks: Karamalos at Ta Pikridiou, the other [?] at the monastery of Stoudios. The island of Lemnos was also taken [?] by the Hagarenes, who carried off many captives. At the procession of the great feast of Pentecost (82), Emperor Leo came to St Mokios and was making his entrance. As he came near the solea, someone stepped out from the ambo and struck him on the head with a strong, thick staff. If a polykandelon had not checked and weakened the force of the blow, it would have killed him. Blood poured heavily from the emperor's head, and confusion and flight broke out among the officials, and many people were killed in it. His brother Alexander had pretended to be ill and had not gone down for the entrance, so he came under suspicion of having contrived this plot. Samonas was not there either; he had gone to bring [?] to the palace. The man who struck the emperor was seized and interrogated, and he endured many tortures and punishments for many days. Since he named no one, in the end his hands and feet were cut off and he was burned in the Sphendone of the Hippodrome. From then on that procession was discontinued. Some time later Mark, a most learned man who was steward of that church, came up. He was the one who had completed the tetraodion of the lord Kosmas for Holy Saturday. Dining with the emperor at his table, he [?] the emperor that the feast had been discontinued (83). But the [?] such a procession...

When the emperor refused, Mark said: "It was foretold by the prophet David that you would suffer this, my lord, and he prophesied it when he said, 'How much evil the enemy has done in your sanctuary,' and, 'Those who hate you have boasted in the midst of your feast.' And from now on, my lord, you are to hold the empire for ten years." And so it happened, for he died on the very day on which he had been struck. Zoe, the emperor's fourth wife, was in the palace with the emperor but uncrowned (84). The emperor made an excursion to the market [?] of Botiou (85) to dedicate the monastery of his protovestiarios Christopher. Then news came that the Hagarene fleet was sailing up against Constantinople with the man from Tripoli. So the emperor sent [?] the drungarios of the fleet with the whole fleet and the strategoi against the man from Tripoli. They could not stand up to him in battle and turned back empty-handed. He went on ahead of them (86) and got as far as Parion. When the emperor learned this, he fell into deep despondency. He sent Himerios the protasekretis as commander of the fleet against the man from Tripoli, but they did not dare at all [and neither did he] to come near the Hagarene fleet. By the judgments of God this same Leo of Tripoli turned back and went to Thessalonica. He besieged it and took it together with his general Leo Chatzilakios, and he carried out great slaughter and took many captives. A certain koubikoularios named Rhodophyles had been sent to Sicily on some business, carrying a hundred pounds of gold. He happened to fall ill on the road and went into Thessalonica to bathe and recover his strength. He was seized by Leo (87) and died after being tortured at length. Symeon the asekretis, who later became patrician and protasekretis, was passing through, and he picked up the gold and the gifts that Rhodophyles had left on the road. When Symeon learned that the man from Tripoli was going to destroy the city, he informed him that he could take gold and [spare] the city [?]. He persuaded him, received his word, and agreed to give the man from Tripoli gold to leave the city alone, and that is what happened. Samonas, on the pretext of going out to his monastery at Damatrys [?], took flight with his money and his horses, hamstringing the public horses. When the emperor learned of this, he sent the hetaireiarch [?] Basil Kamateros and George Krenites after him to catch him. When Samonas [Notes: (84) Cedrenus: [?] for a long time with him [?]. (86) [?] came [?]]

wanted to cross the Halys, the drungarios Nikephoros, known as Kaminas, caught up with him and would not let him cross. Samonas made him many promises but could not persuade him, so he took refuge at Siricha [variant: Sericha], at the precious Cross, pretending that he had come out of devotion to the Cross. Then Constantine, son of Doukas, caught up with him, took him, and brought him back to the city. The emperor ordered him to be held in the house of Bardas the Caesar. He questioned Constantine, son of Doukas, about him, and learned that he really had been fleeing to Syria. He then instructed Doukas not to say this before the senate when they questioned him (88), but to say that Samonas had gone to Siricha to pray, because the emperor wanted to be reconciled with him. So, summoning Constantine, son of Doukas, before the [?], he said: "By God and by my head, was Samonas fleeing or not?" Constantine had earlier told the emperor that he would say what he was told as long as he was not put on oath. When he heard the oath, he declared before everyone that Samonas had been fleeing to Syria. The emperor dismissed him in anger, and Samonas spent four months in the house of Bardas. He was reconciled on the emperor's [?] (89). At that time a comet also appeared, sending its rays toward the east, and it was visible for forty days and nights. Leo had a son, Constantine, by Zoe, his fourth wife. The boy was baptized at holy [?] [Theophany] by Patriarch Nicholas in the Great Church, and Alexander [?] and all the high officials received him from the font. After the feast the emperor was married to Zoe by Thomas, a priest, who was deposed. The emperor proclaimed this Zoe Augusta. For this reason the patriarch barred the emperor from entering the church, so he passed along the right side as far as the mitatorion and never went through the customary way. Samonas was appointed parakoimomenos because he was the emperor's accomplice in all his lawlessness and wickedness, and they began to scheme against the Church. They summoned Patriarch Nicholas on the first of February and pleaded with him at length to receive the emperor, but they could not persuade him. From the [?] banqueting hall they put him through the Boukoleon into a small boat and took him across to Hieria. From there he went on foot as far as Galakrenai, with snow [?]. In his place was ordained [Notes: (88) "when he is questioned by them", when he says [?] questioned [?]... from the synopsis in the curatoria [?]... a short time having passed [?]... Also Anonymous, "of time [?]"... from the cited Cedrenus.]

Euthymios the synkellos, a man of priestly dignity, very temperate and devout. They say he accepted this because of a divine revelation, since the emperor was planning to promulgate a heresy and a law allowing a man (91) to have three or four wives, and many very learned men were helping him in this [God forbid]. In the month of June Emperor Leo was invited by Constantine Lips to his monastery at Merdosangaris, to perform its dedication and dine there. Then the wind called Lips arose and blew violently until the third hour. It shook and rocked houses and churches, so that everyone fled to open places saying it was the end of the world, until God in his love for mankind ended the destruction with rain. The emperor appointed Himerios, logothete of the drome, commander of the whole fleet, because the Hagarene fleet had put out against the Romans. Andronikos the doux also received orders to join the logothete Himerios on the ships and make war on the Hagarenes. Samonas, however, was Andronikos's implacable enemy. Ever since his own flight he had been constantly plotting against him and scheming to harm him by every means and with all his zeal. He got someone to write secretly to Andronikos: "Do not go aboard the ships, or you will be seized by Himerios. Samonas has advised the emperor to have you seized and blinded by him." So although Himerios urged Andronikos again and again to board the ships against the Hagarenes (92), who were pressing hard, [he refused]. Himerios alone joined battle with the Hagarenes on the feast of Saint Thomas and won a great victory. When Andronikos learned of this, he gave up hope, went off with his kinsmen, and seized the fortress of Kabala, breaking into open rebellion. Samonas could then say to the emperor: "Did I not tell you, my lord, that the doux was a rebel against you?" At once the emperor sent Gregoras, domestic of the scholai, known as Iberitzes, who was Andronikos's relative by marriage, to fight him. When Andronikos learned this, and that Patriarch Nicholas [had been driven out] of the church, he fled to the Hagarenes with his kinsmen, his children, and the friends who had come out [Notes: (91) Anonymous: "that men should have a wife" [?]. What if [?] "not having consented to do this" [?]]

[?] then against the Romans. And he was received by the great emir. The emperor Leo was grieved about Andronikos, and often planned to send him a signed letter, as Theophilos had once done for Manuel [?]. Some advised the emperor to treat one of the Saracens of the praetorium kindly and send him to Syria with a signed letter. The emperor did this: he wrote in cinnabar and sent the letter, sealed with a golden bull, inside a small loaf of bread. When the Saracen came out from the emperor, Samonas called him over and said: "Do you know what you are holding?" (he said this because of the wax) "The ruin of Syria." He gave him money and gifts and told him to put it into the hands of the vizier. The man went and did so. Andronikos was seized and put in chains with all his relatives. When he learned that this had happened to him through the treachery of Samonas, he was forced to apostatize, he and those with him. After that his son Constantine and the rest, knowing that Andronikos could not possibly get out, followed his advice and not long afterward fled on their own. Remarkably, they got out of Syria into Roman territory. They had to fight their way through the countryside, and only a few, with his son Constantine, barely escaped. From Tarsus there came to the City, for an exchange of prisoners, both Abelbakes the old man and the father of Samonas. The emperor saw them and received them in the Magnaura with display, honour and glory. He also decorated the Great Church with costly ornaments and showed all the precious vessels to the Hagarenes. This was unworthy of an emperor and of a Christian state, that the holy vessels of God should be seen by the heathen. The father of Samonas wanted to live with the emperor and with his son and to remain in Roman territory. But Samonas advised him, saying: "Hold on to the faith you have, and I, if I can, will come to you instead." On the day of Pentecost the emperor Leo had his son Constantine crowned by the patriarch Euthymius. Samonas gave Constantine, a man of his who had earlier served Basil the magistros and kanikleios, to serve Zoe Augusta. The emperor Leo and the Augusta grew fond of him. For this reason Samonas was very jealous of him and slandered him, saying that he was sleeping with the Augusta. So the emperor [?] had him tonsured a monk in the monastery of Saint Tarasius through Barnas [?]. [?] … "he apostatized": the Anonymous and Cedrenus [?] … omitting what follows, "he received".

[Later] he ordered Samonas to take him into his own monastery, called Speira, because he wanted to take him back again. So he went out in procession to Damatrys and had lunch in Samonas's monastery. There he saw Constantine and at once ordered [?] him. He dressed him in secular clothes, and Constantine entertained the emperor at a banquet and returned with him to the palace. Samonas saw that the emperor's affection for him was growing, so he plotted with the great koitonites and Michael Steridon. They produced a pamphlet full of abuse against the emperor, written and composed by the Rhodian, who was Samonas's notary. When the emperor came into the Great Church he found it in the place where he prayed, in the mitatorion. He picked it up and read it, and was in great distress, trying to find out who had done it. There was also an eclipse of the moon, and the emperor ordered the astronomers of the day to say what it portended. When the metropolitan Pantaleon, a friend of Samonas, came in to the [emperor?], Samonas asked him: "Against whom is the harm?" He said: "Against you. But if you get past the thirteenth of June, after that you will suffer no harm." The astronomers told the emperor that the moon portended harm to the second in rank. The emperor took this to mean his brother Alexander. After this Tziredon told the emperor privately: "Samonas made the pamphlet." At once the emperor sent Samonas down to his own house, first had him tonsured, and took him off to the monastery of the patriarch Euthymius. Later, after he had been slandered again, they took him away to the monastery of Martinakes. The emperor made Constantine parakoimomenos and built him a monastery at Nosiai. They went there together with the patriarch Euthymius and dedicated it. In the month of October there was a sea battle between Himerios the logothete and the Hagarenes Damian and Leo, at a time when Romanos, who later became emperor, was general at Samos. Himerios was defeated and barely [escaped?], since almost everyone there was in danger. The emperor Leo began to suffer from a disease of the bowels, so that he could not come out to the Magnaura to deliver the address at the beginning of Lent. There was also a fire in the candle-makers' workshops of the Great Church, and all the archives and the sakelle were burned. On the eleventh of May the emperor Leo died, having designated his brother Alexander as his successor. They say that when he saw him coming in to him, he said: "Here is the bad time, after the thirteen months." He begged and entreated him earnestly to look after his son Constantine.

ALEXANDER. Alexander reigned one year and twenty-four days together with Constantine, the son of Leo. He sent for Nicholas and brought him back from Galakrenai. He deposed the patriarch Euthymius and enthroned the same Nicholas a second time. Alexander held a silention and a synod in the Magnaura, bringing Euthymius from the monastery of Agathou. Sitting together with the patriarch Nicholas, they carried out his deposition. They disgracefully plucked out the venerable beard of that holy and admirable man and inflicted other outrages and punishments on him, which that honourable and holy man endured quietly and meekly. He later died at Agathou and was buried in his own monastery in the City, the monastery of Psamathia. Leo his brother had suspected Alexander while he was still alive, and because of this Alexander always spent his time hunting and in the palaces outside the City. He did none of an emperor's work but lived in luxury, debauchery and drunkenness, and always gave himself to these things. So he made the priest John, surnamed Lazares, rhaiktor, and after Alexander's death this John came to a miserable end. They say that he also made Gabrielopoulos and Basilitzes, men of the Slav nation, very rich from the palace funds. They say that he even wanted to make this Basil[itzes] emperor, since he himself was childless, and to make Constantine, the son of Leo, a eunuch. He planned this often, but it was frustrated by those whom Leo had favoured. Sometimes they pointed out that the boy was only an infant, sometimes that he was sickly. In his time a comet appeared in the west for fifteen days. They said it was called xiphias, "the swordfish", and that it would bring bloodshed in the City. He gave himself over to impostors and sorcerers, who persuaded him that "The talismanic statue of the boar in the Hippodrome is bound up with you and your life." They were hinting at the senseless swine himself. Taken in by them, he restored genitals and teeth to the boar, since these were missing. Trusting in his delusion, he held races and decorated the Hippodrome with the vestments and chandeliers of the churches, and he lit up the statues. For this reason the hand of God was taken away from him, because he had given God's honour to idols. When Himerios the logothete returned after his defeat by the Hagarenes, Alexander sent and confined him in the palace monastery called Ka[?]. He threatened him, saying that Himerios had been his enemy in the time of his brother Leo. Himerios fell ill from his great distress and, after being confined for six months, he died. Sy- [?] In the Anonymous and Cedrenus: "brought into the City, he is buried in his monastery of Psamathia." [?] After the word "engaged": "having ruled alone, he accomplished nothing noble or worth mentioning" [?].

-meon, the ruler of Bulgaria, sent to Alexander about peace. [?] Symeon prepared to take up arms against the Christians. The emperor Alexander, having had lunch and drunk wine in the heat of the dog days, went down to play ball. He was struck by a God-sent sword. He went back up with blood pouring from his nose and genitals, and two days later he died. As guardians he left the patriarch Nicholas, Stephen the magistros, John Eladas the magistros, John the rhaiktor, Euthymius, Basilitzes and Gabrielopoulos, and he left the empire to Constantine, the son of Leo. Alexander was laid in the tombs with his father.

CONSTANTINE. When his father Leo died, Constantine was still a child, in his seventh year. His uncle Alexander left him in the empire under guardians, and he reigned under his guardians and with his mother. Then, together with his father-in-law Romanos and subordinate to him, he reigned another twenty-[?] years. As sole ruler he reigned fifteen years, so that the whole length of his reign was fifty-five years. The patriarch Nicholas took control of the palace, managed public affairs and looked after the business of the empire day by day. While the empire was in this state, some of the magnates in the City who were fond of Constantine Doukas, the domestic of the Scholai, sent him word. He was brave, sensible and well able to govern the empire, they said, so he should come in and take control of it without any trouble. He had dreamed of this before and had always longed for the crown. So he reached the capital as fast as he could with a fair number of picked men from the armies. He came in by night through a postern gate and stayed awake with his companions in the house of Michael the protovestiarios, which was near the acropolis and had belonged to Michael's father-in-law Gregoras. Niketas the asekretis, who later became protonotarios, reported Constantine's arrival to the patrikios Constantine Helladikos. Both of them came that same night to Constantine Doukas. [?] … of peace, so that he might greet [?] and be shown friendship and honour, just as under the emperor Leo. But he, overcome by folly and senselessness, sent the envoys away in disgrace [?]. So when the peace had broken down, Sy[meon] [?] … domestic of the Scholai, Constan-

After taking counsel, while it was still dark and before day had broken, they seized the gate of the Hippodrome with torches, a large crowd and weapons, acclaiming Constantine as emperor. There his groom was killed by those inside the gates of the Hippodrome. So Constantine was not admitted there. Driven off, he behaved as if possessed by some frenzied demon, his mind unsettled [?] by his passion for the throne. He withdrew from the Hippodrome gloomy and downcast, taking the groom's death as a bad omen. From there, still being acclaimed, he came to the place called the Chalke, went in through the iron gate and reached the Exkoubitoi. The magistros John Eladas picked out men from the Hetaireia and the oarsmen and sent them armed against the Doukas. They came as far as the Chalke and battle was joined. Many fell on both sides there, cut down by the sword, so many that the place became a pool of blood flowing like a river. Gregoras, the Doukas's son, was killed, along with his cousin Michael and the well-known Kourtikes, the Armenian. When Constantine Doukas learned this, amid the greatest confusion he spurred on his horse. But it slipped on the paving slabs there and threw its rider to the ground, for all the others had scattered. Someone found him lying on the ground, left alone [?], and cut off his head with a sword. When this was over, his father-in-law Gregoras the magistros fled to the Holy Wisdom of God together with Leo, whom they called Choirosphaktes. They dragged them out of there by force, dressed them in rags, sat them on a donkey and paraded them through the middle of the City. Then they took them to the monastery of Dalmatos, the one called Katadike, and shut them up there. They blinded Leo Katakalitzes and Abessalom, the son of Arotras, and sent them into exile. Philotheos the eparch beheaded Constantine, the son of Eulimpios, and others with him at the Sphendone of the Hippodrome. He searched long and hard for Niketas the asekretis and Constantine Lips but did not find them, since they had fled. That [?] and those with him, many of them and brave men, he impaled, every one, on forked stakes from Damalis at Chrysopolis as far as [?]. And many [?] mercilessly [?] … taking him from there … the Hippodrome … in the monastery of Spoudaios [?] … Constantine with Helladikos [?] …

and these so-called guardians would have killed them without cause if some of the judges had not checked their unjust rage. They said to them: "Since the emperor is a child, how do you dare to do such things without his command?" They tonsured the Doukas's wife and sent her away to her house in Paphlagonia, and they also castrated his son. In the month of August Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, marched against the Romans with a huge host and reached Constantinople. He laid siege to it and built a palisade around it from Blachernai as far as the so-called Golden Gate, buoyed up by the hope of taking it with no trouble at all. But he found out how strong the walls were and how well they were secured by the large numbers of defenders and the stone-throwing engines. Disappointed in his hopes, he withdrew to the place called the Hebdomon and asked for a peace treaty. The guardians welcomed peace most gladly, and Symeon sent his magistros Theodore to negotiate its terms. The patriarch Nicholas, Stephen and John the magistros took the emperor with them and went to Blachernai. They brought in Symeon's two sons, who feasted with the emperor in the palace. The patriarch Nicholas went out to Symeon, and Symeon bowed his head to him. The patriarch said a prayer and placed his own veil on Symeon's head in place of a crown. Symeon and his sons were treated with countless rich gifts and returned to their own country, though they parted without agreement on the peace. The emperor Constantine was a child and kept asking for his mother, whom the emperor Alexander had already put out of the palace, so they brought her back up again. Once she had control of the empire, she brought up to the palace Constantine the parakoimomenos and the brothers Constantine and Anastasios, called the Gongylioi. On the advice of John Eladas they put down Alexander's intimates: John the rhaiktor, the man called Gabrielopoulos, Basilitzes and the rest. Zoe Augusta appointed Theophylaktos Dominikos as hetaireiarch. John Eladas fell ill and went down from the palace. When he reached Blachernai his illness grew worse and he died. On the advice of Dominikos and those with him [?], she angrily took charge of the affairs of the empire and said that she would look after them. The Bulgarian Symeon was plundering Thrace again, and the Augusta and those in authority were worried about how to put a stop to his arrogance. John Bogas asked [?] … many of the senators [?] … and her son Stephen.

to be made patrikios, promising to bring the Pechenegs. His request was granted, and after receiving many gifts he set off for the land of the Pechenegs. He took hostages from there and brought them to the City, since the Pechenegs had agreed to cross over and make war on Symeon. Ashot, the son of the prince of princes, also came to the City. He was a man very famous for his skill. They say that he could hold an iron rod by its ends in both hands and bend it with his enormous strength into the shape of a circle, the stubborn nature of the iron giving way to the force of his hands. They received him with great honour when he arrived and sent him back to his own country. In September of the third indiction Pankratoukas the Armenian betrayed Adrianople to Symeon. Not long afterward Zoe sent Basil, the patrikios and kanikleios, and Niketas Helladikos, the protospatharios, with many gifts, and they took the city back. An emir also came to the island of Strobelos with warships and a large force. He would have taken it if he had not fallen ill and died. The inhabitants of Hellas and Athens were constantly abused by Chases, the son of Iouba. Unable to bear his debauchery and greed any longer, they stoned him to death, a wretched death, inside the sanctuary of the church in Athens. The empress Zoe saw Symeon's arrogance and his attacks on the Christians. She took counsel with those in authority to arrange an exchange of prisoners and a peace with the Hagarenes, and to bring the whole army of the East across to fight Symeon and destroy him. So the patrikios John Rhadenos was sent to Syria to make the exchange, and Michael Toxaras crossed to Thrace, Leo Phokas being domestic at the time. In Thrace Constantine, the protopapas of the palace, called Kephalas, and Constantine of Malelias brought out the venerable and life-giving Wood. Everyone venerated it and swore to die together with one another, and then they set out in full force against the Bulgarians. John Grapson commanded the tagma of the Exkoubitoi, and the son of Maroules that of the Hikanatoi. The generals were Romanos Argyros, his brother Leo, and Bardas Phokas, who was joined by Melias with the Armenians, and also the other generals of all the themes. Besides the others there was also the patrikios Constantine Lips, who advised Leo the domestic in every matter. On the twentieth of August of the fifth indiction the battle between [the Romans and the] Bulga[rians] [?] … the customary distribution of pay among the tagmata. Having received these, they crossed into Thrace with the themes. [?] … of the Scholai: the Anonymous and Cedrenus.

[…] of the Bulgarians and the Romans had been joined at the river Achelous, and (how unsearchable and untraceable are the judgments of God!) the Romans were routed with their whole army. There was flight and a dreadful wailing: some were trampled by one another, others were slain by the enemy, and there was such a shedding of blood as had never happened since the beginning of time. Leo the domestic escaped by fleeing to Mesembria, but Constantine Lips was slain, and John Grapson, and many other officers. At that time Romanos, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, was also sent with the whole fleet to the river Danube to help Leo Phokas. But Romanos and John Bogas fell into quarrels and disputes, and the Pechenegs, seeing them fighting and at odds with each other, withdrew to their own lands, and the war came to an end. When Romanos and Bogas [above: Bogas] returned to the City, charges were brought against them, and they put the droungarios Romanos in such danger that a sentence was passed condemning him to lose his eyes, on the grounds that through negligence, or rather malice, he had not ferried the Pechenegs across, but had withdrawn too quickly and had not even taken the fugitives on board his ships. And he would have suffered this, had not the condemnation been overturned by Constantine Gongyles and Stephen the magistros, who had influence with the Augusta. The Bulgarians, elated by their victory, marched as far as the City, and Leo, domestic of the Schools, John the hetaireiarches, and Nicholas the son of Doukas went out with a very large force against the Bulgarians to a place in Thrace called Katasyrtai. But the Bulgarians fell on them unexpectedly at night; the domestic fled, and Nicholas the son of Doukas was slain, and many others with him. Then Theodore, tutor of the emperor Constantine, seeing that Constantine the parakoimomenos was appropriating the imperial power for his own son-in-law Leo, advised the emperor Constantine to promote the droungarios Romanos, as a servant of his father and well disposed toward him, so that he might have him at his side and Romanos might protect him whenever he needed an ally and helper. Although he was approached about this many times, Romanos declined. So the emperor Constantine wrote out a short letter in his own hand, secured it with his signature, and sent it to him; and Romanos, taking it in hand, (18) [?] Cedrenus: 'at the Achelous' [?] 'by force' the Bulgarians. Certainly 'the Romans' [?]. [?] John Bogas to bring down the Pechenegs, the droungarios Romanos having been ordered to ferry them across [?]—

promised to make the attack on the parakoimomenos Constantine and his relatives, as was needed. As this rumor spread, and the parakoimomenos Constantine was pressing Romanos to set out with the fleet, Romanos pleaded that he was unable to sail because the fleet had not received its customary pay. While Romanos was fitting out and preparing the ships, Constantine the parakoimomenos came out to hurry him into sailing. Romanos met him with the bearing of a servant and promised to carry out the order eagerly. When the parakoimomenos was about to go back, and asked Romanos whether he had handsome and brave men fit to row the imperial trireme, Romanos at once signaled with his hand to those who stood ready nearby to come. They, knowing the plan, and being already very close to Romanos's dromon, seized him with their hands and shouted, 'Take him!' At once they seized him, carried him into the trireme of the droungarios Romanos, and held him under guard. There was no one to defend him, since all his companions took to flight. When Zoe Augusta learned of this, she summoned the patriarch Nicholas and her magnates and sent them to Romanos, wishing to learn what had happened. But when they crossed over, the people drove them off with stones. At dawn Zoe came out onto the terrace of the Boukoleon and cried out to her son and to everyone, 'How has this rebellion come about?' Theodore, tutor of the emperor Constantine, said to her, 'These things have happened because Leo Phokas has destroyed the Romans, and Constantine the parakoimomenos the palace.' The emperor took the patriarch Nicholas and Stephen the magistros to stay with him in the palace, drawing the authority to himself away from his mother. The next day he sent John Toubakes to remove Zoe Augusta from the palace. But she clung to her son with wailing and tears and moved him to a son's compassion and pity, so that the emperor said, 'Let my mother stay with me.' And at that word they released her. The emperor and the patriarch summoned John Garidas and appointed him domestic of the Schools, fearing that Leo Phokas might turn to rebellion. But Phokas would not consent to this unless they appointed his wife's brother Theodore Zouphinezer, and his own son Symeon, as hetaireiarches. Having been given assurances on oath by them, he went down to his house. Immediately they removed his relatives from the palace. When these came to him, (25) Theophanes [?]: 'to those who were ready at hand.' Anonymous: '[?] having happened… since this man, walking behind the parakoimomenos Constantine, seized him with his…'

and he saw them, trembling and bewilderment seized him. So he at once went out to Romanos and told him what he had suffered. He was reconciled with him, and they gave and received oaths that the two would have one soul; he became of one mind and one spirit with him, so that they also agreed to make a marriage alliance, tightening the bond of affection still further by this. On the twenty-fourth of March, Romanos sent John, a priest of his household and most trusted, and Theodore called Matzoukes to the palace to make his defense, saying: 'What I have done is not rebellion; rather, suspecting the designs of Phokas and fearing that he might attempt some revolution against the emperor, I resolved for this reason to come up to the palace and guard the emperor.' When the patriarch Nicholas did not approve of this, word was sent to Romanos by Theodore, the tutor already mentioned, to come with the whole fleet to the Boukoleon. After deliberating with those around him [for the struggle (?) held him] (24), on the day of the Annunciation of the all-holy Theotokos (it was a Thursday) he came armed with the fleet to the Boukoleon. At once Stephen the magistros [was expelled?] from the palace, and the patrician Niketas, Romanos's fellow father-in-law, went up into the palace and brought the patriarch Nicholas out of it. Those in the palace, having received assurances on oath from Romanos, sent him the precious cross and [?]; and having confirmed them with an oath, he went up with them and a few others into the palace to do obeisance to the emperor. Entering the church at the Pharos with him, and giving and receiving pledges of loyalty, he was at once appointed by him magistros and grand hetaireiarches. Immediately an imperial order was issued to Leo Phokas, charging him on no account to contemplate any sedition, but to rest for a while in his own house. Likewise Constantine the parakoimomenos was ordered (25) to write similar letters, instructing him to plan nothing hostile but to be in submission to the emperor Constantine. Andrew, primikerios of the imperial wardrobe, took these and brought them to him in Cappadocia; and he received them, went off to his own house, and kept quiet. On the fifth [?] of the holy Fast, in the month of April, the pledge of marriage was given by the emperor Constantine to Helena, the daughter of Romanos, and on the Tuesday of Easter week, called the Tuesday of Galilee, they were blessed and crowned [?]. (24) [?] for not thus 'τὸ ἆγον', or 'τὸ ἀγών'. (25) [?] Constantine the parakoimomenos.

together with her by the patriarch Nicholas, and he promoted Romanos to basileopator, and in his place he appointed Romanos's son Christopher hetaireiarches. Not long afterward Leo Phokas, deceived by some of the officers and men of his own regiments, was moved to rebellion with a very large force. He sent to win over to his side Constantine the parakoimomenos, Constantine and Anastasios Gongyles, who were brothers, and Constantine Malelias the asekretis, assuring them all and affirming that he was making this uprising on behalf of the emperor Constantine. But Romanos the basileopator had chrysobulls drawn up and signed, in the name of the emperor Constantine, which set out the overthrow of this plot and stated that those who abandoned Phokas and fled to the emperor were on the emperor's side. He gave them to a certain Anna, a shameless and bold woman, and to a cleric named Michael, and sent them into that very camp. They took them and distributed them throughout the whole army. Michael was detected, mercilessly beaten by Phokas, and had his nose and ears cut off; afterwards he received a fitting reward from Romanos, as did the woman sent with him. The first to desert Phokas and run over to Romanos was the son of Barymichael, who became the beginning of the collapse of this rebellion and usurpation, and with him Balantios; both were tourmarchai. Leo Phokas arrived at Chrysopolis with a very large and heavily armed force and drew up battle lines from the stone Heifer [Damalis] to Chalcedon, frightening those in the City. So Romanos sent Symeon, the official in charge of the inkstand, in a dromon, carrying a signed statement of the emperor Constantine which declared as follows: 'Having found no one among my subjects a more watchful and faithful guardian of my reign than Romanos, I have entrusted my protection to him, after God, and have decided to regard him as a father, since he has shown me a mother's tenderness and a parent's affection. As for this Leo Phokas, I always suspected him of plotting against my reign, and now I have found him by his very deeds to be a plotter, rising up like a usurper against my rule. Therefore I do not want him to be domestic from now on, nor do I say that he carried out this rebellion with my counsel, but that he made this attack of his own will, appropriating the empire for himself.' When this was read out to the troops, they all began to withdraw and go over to the basileopator Romanos. Phokas, finding himself in a hopeless position and in despair, having lost every hope, took to flight, and in despair came to the fortress of Ateous [?] (27) 'to the fortress of Ateous [?]': thus [?]

and was not received; and as he fled he was captured at a place called Goeleon. Romanos sent John Toubakes and Leo, his own relative, to bring him into the City. But they, having taken him, blinded him, although they had received no order concerning him, but had done this of their own accord, so that even the basileopator Romanos was angered at it. In the month of August the plot of Constantine Ktematenos, David Kamoulianos, and Michael, curator of the Mangana, was denounced; they were beaten and their property confiscated, they were paraded through the middle of the City, and they were sent into exile. They also brought Leo, magistros and domestic of the Schools, into the City, and he was paraded through the middle of the marketplace seated on a mule. Zoe Augusta too was caught plotting against Romanos by means of poisoned food prepared by Theokletos, notary of the hypourgia [the imperial table service]; they removed her from the palace, took her to the Petrion, and tonsured her in the monastery of St Euphemia. Theodore, tutor of the emperor Constantine, and Symeon his brother were invited to lunch by Theophylact, patrician and count of the stable. While they were eating, John Kourkouas the droungarios came in with a large force, seized them, and exiled them to their estates in the Opsikion, as men plotting against Romanos. [He was honored ?] on the [twenty-]fourth [?] of September with the rank of Caesar, and on the seventeenth of December, the Sunday of the Forefathers of the Lord, he was crowned with the imperial diadem by the emperor Constantine and the patriarch Nicholas; and on the day of the holy Lights he crowned his wife Theodora. On the seventeenth of May, in the fifth indiction, Christopher, the son of Romanos, was proclaimed emperor; he was crowned on the twentieth of the same month by the emperor Constantine, on the day of holy Pentecost, and these two alone took part in the same procession [?]. In the month of July of the eighth indiction, on the Lord's day [?], the union of the Church was brought about by Romanos, and all the metropolitans and clergy who had been divided between the patriarch Nicholas and Euthymios were united. On the eighth of February, in the [?] indiction, Romanos sent and banished Stephen the magistros, the son of Kalomaria, to the island of Antigonos, since he had been accused of aspiring to the throne; he first had him tonsured, together with Theophanes Teicheiotes and Paul the orphanotrophos, his men. The emperor Romanos held a review in the Tribunal, with everyone gathered there under arms. While the muster was taking place (29)

Romanos and Constantine suddenly returned with great speed to the palace, for the plot of Arsenios himself and of Paul the manglabites had been denounced by Leo, a man of Arsenios; these were beaten, their property was confiscated, and they were exiled. At that time John, the priest and rhaiktor, held power at court; he made Leo, the son of the Armenian [?], a hebdomarios (31), attaching him to the emperor. When the Bulgarians again marched out as far as Katasyrtai after the [?] of the domestic Adralestos (32), Pothos Argyros was appointed domestic of the Schools. He went out with the tagmata as far as Thermopolis and sent Michael, son of Moroleon, who was topoteretes (33), to spy on the Bulgarians. But Michael fell unexpectedly into their ambush; he killed many of the Bulgarians, but was himself wounded and died in the City. At that time Theokletos [?] of the hypourgia denounced the plot against the emperor Romanos by Anastasios, sakellarios and head of the gold workshop, Theodoretos the koitonites, Demetrios, imperial notary of the private treasury, and Nicholas Kouboutzes (34). Convicted, they were beaten and paraded through the Mese. Theodoretos was beaten separately in the so-called Trikonchos of the palace, and he too was exiled. The sakellarios Anastasios he had tonsured in the monastery of the Elegmoi (35), where he also died. Seizing on this pretext, Romanos demoted the emperor Constantine (36) and made him second, advancing himself to first place. Symeon again campaigned against the Romans, and sending a host of Bulgarians, ordered them to drive against the City as quickly as possible. Passing through the mountains, they came as far as [?]. When the emperor Romanos learned of this attack, [fearing] that they might come down and burn the palaces of Pegai and the Stenon, he sent John the rhaiktor together with Leo and Pothos, who were called the Argyroi, with a host drawn from the imperial troops (37), the hetaireia, and the tagmata; with them was Alexios Mousele, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, with his men. It was the fifth week of the Fast. They drew up (30) 'of Paul the manglabites': Cedrenus, Anonymous [?]. (31) [?] (33) [?] taxiarch, that is, a tribune [?]. (34) Kouboutzes, and Theodotos the protokarabos.

Chronography. the troops (38); and when the Bulgarians appeared above them under arms, raising an inarticulate and terrifying shout, John the rhaiktor fled at once, and Photeinos the son of Platypodes, fighting to protect him, was slain, together with many others. John barely escaped and boarded a dromon. Alexios Mousele the droungarios also came fleeing in full armor, and being unable to climb all the way up the dromon's gangway, fell into the sea with [?] and drowned. The Argyroi escaped by fleeing into the fort. The Bulgarians, with no one to stop them, set fire to the palaces of Pegai and burned the whole Stenon. On the twentieth of February in the tenth indiction, Theodora, the wife of Romanos, died, and her body was laid to rest in his house (39). In the same month Sophia, the wife of the emperor Christopher, was crowned. At that time the kouropalates Ashot came to the City and passed through the middle of it, which had been splendidly adorned (40); they brought him into God's Holy Wisdom, and having seen its beauty and size and marveled greatly at its costly adornment, he returned again to

In the month of June, when the Bulgarians campaigned again, came as far as the palaces of St Theodora, and set them on fire, the emperor Romanos rose up and summoned the commanders of the tagmata, among them the man called Saktikes, and he exhorted them and urged them to go out against the enemy and fight for their fatherland. They agreed readily to die on behalf of the Christians. So the next day the aforementioned Saktikes armed himself and proved his loyalty and courage to be genuine. For he got behind the Bulgarians, fell upon their camp, and slaughtered everyone he found there. When the Bulgarians learned what had happened, they returned to the camp, and when battle was joined they routed Saktikes, who had only a few men. After fighting bravely and killing many, he could no longer hold out against the multitude of the enemy, so he gave his horse its head and rode off in flight. But as he was crossing a river that flowed past there, his horse stuck in the mud, and he was wounded in the buttocks and the thigh. When the horse had been pulled out of the mud with difficulty, he escaped as far as Blachernae, and was laid in the chapel of the holy Soros; but since the wound was mortal, he died during the night. A certain Adrian the Chaldean [?] … to [?] and lower-lying places of Pegai [?] … Having adorned it and wrapped it in gold-woven robes and with adornment [?]

and Tatzates, a very rich Armenian, with the agreement and on the advice of Bardas Boilas, who was strategos in Chaldia, prepared a usurpation and rebellion against the emperor Romanos, seizing the fortress called Paipert. John Kourkouas, domestic of the Schools, defeated them and captured some of them; the most prominent he blinded, confiscating their property (41). Tatzates fled to another very strong fort, and having received a promise that he would suffer no harm, he came into the City; he was honored with the rank of manglabites and lived under guard in the house of the Mangana. But he plotted to escape, was caught, and was deprived of his eyes. Bardas Boilas they tonsured as a monk. When the patrician named Moroleon (42) was strategos of Adrianople, a man most able and skillful in war, who had performed many feats of valor against Bulgaria, Symeon the Bulgarian surrounded that city with his whole army, threw a palisade around it, and besieged it vigorously. When the grain ran out for those in the city and a severe famine pressed them (for they had no way of getting provisions from anywhere), pressed by want they surrendered themselves and their strategos to the Bulgarians. Symeon, having taken him prisoner, bound his whole body in chains and killed him with a bitter death. Then, handing the guard of the city over to Bulgarians, he withdrew. When Leo of Tripoli set out against the Romans with a large force and warships and arrived at the island of Lemnos, John Rhadenos, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, suddenly attacked him. When battle was joined, by God's help the Hagarenes under Leo were routed; the Tripolitan alone escaped by flight. In the month of September of the second indiction, Symeon, ruler of Bulgaria, campaigned with his whole army against Constantinople. He plundered Thrace and Macedonia, set everything on fire, laid waste, and cut down the trees. When he reached Blachernae, he asked that the patriarch Nicholas and some of the magnates be sent out to him, so that he could confer with them about peace. So both sides took hostages, and first the patriarch Nicholas went out, then Michael Stypiotes the patrician, and John the Mystikos, who held power at court. For John the rhaiktor had already been slandered to the emperor, had pleaded illness and left the palace, and had been tonsured in his own monastery (43) near the Galakrenai. So they talked with Symeon about peace; he sent them away, but asked to see the emperor Romanos himself, for he had been informed by many people of his prudence, courage, and intelligence. The emperor (41) But the poor and obscure [he let go] unharmed [?]. (42) 'thus named Moroleon', or rather, to put it more properly, Thumoleon [?] … [?]

[?] rejoiced greatly at this, for he longed for peace and for an end to the bloodshed that went on every day. So he sent men to the shore at Kosmidion and had a very strong landing-stage built out into the sea, so that the imperial trireme could sail out and moor at it. He had it fenced in on every side and ordered a dividing wall to be built across the middle, where the two of them were to talk with each other. But Symeon sent men and burned the church of the most holy Mother of God at Pege and the buildings around it. This made it plain that he had not chosen peace but was deceiving the emperor with empty hopes. The emperor went to Blachernae, and he and Nicholas the patriarch entered the holy reliquary chapel, where he stretched out his hands in prayer. Then he fell on his face and drenched the holy floor with his tears. He begged the all-immaculate Mother of God to soften the unbending and implacable heart of proud Symeon and to win it over to peace. They opened the holy casket in which the venerable veil of the holy Mother of God was kept, and the emperor took it up. Putting on his faith in the spotless Mother of God like a helmet, he left the church protected by sure armour. He equipped the fleet that was with him with shields and weapons and reached the appointed place to speak with Symeon. These events took place on Thursday, the ninth of November, at the fourth hour of the day. Symeon arrived leading a vast multitude. Some had gold shields and gold spears, others silver shields and silver spears, and others were fitted out with every kind of weapon, all of them clad in iron. They kept Symeon in their midst and acclaimed him as emperor in the language of the Romans. All the members of the senate stood on the walls and watched what was happening. Then one could see a truly imperial and lofty soul and marvel at a spirit that could not be daunted. Seeing so great an onrush of enemies, he was not struck with fear, nor did he shrink back or withdraw. He went forward calmly, as though into a crowd of friends, all but offering his own life to the enemy as a ransom for his subjects. He was the first to reach the landing-stage, and there he waited for Symeon. Hostages were taken from both sides, and the Bulgarians searched the landing-stage thoroughly in case there was some trick or ambush. Then Symeon got down from his horse and went in to the emperor. They greeted one another and opened talks about peace. The emperor is said to have spoken to Symeon as follows: "I have heard that you are a God-fearing man and a true Christian, but I see that your deeds in no way match your words. For it is the mark of a God-fearing man and a Christian to embrace peace and love,

since God is love and is called love. But it is the mark of an ungodly and faithless man to delight in slaughter and in blood unjustly shed. If, then, you are a true Christian, as we have been assured, put an end at last to the unjust slaughter and the wicked shedding of blood. Make peace with us Christians, since you yourself are a Christian and bear the name. Do not choose to stain Christian hands with the blood of Christians who share your faith. You too are a man, and you await death, resurrection and judgement. Today you are alive, and tomorrow you will crumble into dust. A single fever will put out all your arrogance. What account, then, will you give to God when you go there, for these unjust slaughters? With what face will you meet the fearsome and just Judge? If you do this because you love wealth, I will give you all you desire and more. Only hold back your hand. Embrace peace and cherish concord, so that you yourself may live a peaceful and untroubled life, and the Christians may at last be freed from their misfortunes. For it is not right for them to take up arms against those who share their faith." Having said this much, the emperor fell silent. Symeon was put to shame by his humility and his words and agreed to make peace. They embraced each other and parted, and the emperor honoured Symeon with magnificent gifts. I will now tell of a portent that occurred at that time, one that seemed strange to those skilled in interpreting such things. They say that while the rulers were talking, two eagles flew above them. They screeched [?], came together, and at once separated. One went toward the City and the other flew off toward Thrace. Those who study such things carefully judged this to be a bad omen, for they said the two would part without reaching an agreement on peace. When Symeon reached his camp [?], he told his nobles about the emperor's wisdom and humility. On the twenty-fifth of December Romanos crowned his sons Stephen and Constantine in the Great Church of God. The patriarch tonsured his son Theophylact as a cleric, ordaining him subdeacon and appointing him synkellos, after he had first passed through the order of subdeacons into the sanctuary. On the twenty-ninth of April Romanos honoured John the Mystikos with the rank of patrikios and anthypatos. On the fifteenth of May in the third indiction the patriarch Nicholas departed this life, having held office for thirteen years in his second term. His body was laid in the monastery of Galakrenai, which he had built. In August Stephen, metropolitan of Amaseia, who was a eunuch, was made patriarch.

In October John the Mystikos, who was also the emperor's chief minister, was accused of aiming at the throne. The patrikios Cosmas, logothete of the drome, had prompted him, and had given him his daughter in marriage. For this reason John was removed from the palace, but he was still allowed to come in, serve the emperor and manage affairs with him, for the emperor was extremely fond of him. But the accusers kept pressing the emperor. He looked into the matter, learned that the charges were true, and intended to arrest John and interrogate him. John learned of this in advance and fled. He reached the place called Monokastanon and was tonsured a monk there. Constantine, son of Boilas, the official in charge of the table, also fled, since he was John's intimate and friend. He reached Olympus and put on the monastic habit. He too was afraid, because he was in John's confidence and shared his secrets. The emperor had the patrikios Cosmas flogged in the Horologion and replaced him. In place of John the Mystikos he promoted Theophanes the protovestiarios as chief minister. At that time there was also a terrible earthquake in the theme of the Thrakesians, and a great and astonishing chasm opened in the earth, so that many villages and churches were swallowed up together with their people. On the twenty-seventh of May in the fifteenth indiction Symeon, ruler of Bulgaria, died. He had appointed as ruler his son Peter, whom he had by his second wife, the sister of George Sursuvul. Symeon also left George as guardian of his children. When the surrounding nations learned of Symeon's death, they planned to make war on the Bulgarians. Famine and locusts were also pressing hard on the Bulgarian nation, and the Bulgarians feared an attack by the Romans. So after taking counsel they marched against the Romans and reached Macedonia. Then they learned that the emperor Romanos was about to march against them. Peter and George secretly sent a monk named Kalokyres, an Armenian by birth, carrying a golden bull. It stated that they not only welcomed peace with the Romans but also wished to conclude a marriage alliance. The emperor received this monk most gladly. He at once sent the monk Theodore Aboukes and the imperial cleric Basil the Rhodian by dromon to Mesembria to discuss peace with the Bulgarians. They arrived and discussed the necessary matters, then set out by land together with Stephen the Bulgarian. George Sursuvul followed after them, and when they reached Constantinople they concluded the peace. They saw Maria, the daughter of the emperor Christopher, and were greatly pleased with her, so they wrote to Peter to come quickly. When Peter the Bulgarian arrived, the emperor Romanos boarded a trireme,

went to Blachernae, and saw and embraced Peter. They discussed the necessary matters with each other and drew up the terms of the peace and the marriage contracts. On the eighth of October the patriarch Stephen went out to the church of the most holy Mother of God at Pege with Theophanes the protovestiarios, Maria the daughter of the emperor Christopher, and the whole senate, and he blessed Peter and Maria. A splendid and lavish banquet was held, and all the usual wedding customs were joyfully carried out. Then Theophanes the protovestiarios went back into the city with Maria, the emperor's daughter. On the third day of the wedding the emperor Romanos gave a splendid feast at the landing-stage of Pegai. The Bulgarians firmly insisted that Christopher should be acclaimed first and only after him Constantine. The emperor gave in to their insistence, and what they asked was done. When everything at the wedding had been completed and Maria was about to set out on the road to Bulgaria, her parents went with her as far as the Hebdomon. They embraced their daughter and shed many tears, as is natural when one loses a beloved child. They embraced their son-in-law, placed her in his hands, and returned to the palace. Maria, now handed over into Bulgarian hands, [set out on] the road to Bulgaria [?]

At that time envoys came to the emperor Romanos from Melitene to make a peace treaty. Not long afterward Apochaps, the descendant of Amer and emir of Melitene, came from Melitene with Apolasar [?], a general of very noble birth and great wealth. Romanos received them with fitting honour, and after making a peace agreement they returned home. But when Apochaps died, a prudent and intelligent man, the people of Melitene broke the peace. The domestic of the scholai, John Kourkouas, marched against them with the themes, and Melias with the Armenians. They reduced Melitene to such straits that it was very quickly sacked and razed to the ground. The emperor made this Melitene into an imperial estate and had many thousands in gold and silver brought from it every year as tribute. Niketas the magistros, father-in-law of the emperor Christopher, was accused of urging Christopher to turn against his own father and drive him from the throne. So they took him out of the city and tonsured him a monk. On the eighth of July in the sixth indiction the patriarch Stephen died. In December they brought in Tryphon, a monk well known for his piety and holiness, and ordained him patriarch. He was to hold office until Theophylact, son of the emperor Romanos, came of age, for they intended

to ordain Theophylact patriarch of Constantinople. On the twenty-fifth of the same month a great winter set in, and the ground stayed frozen for a hundred and twenty days. As a result there was a great famine and so many deaths that the living could not carry out the dead. When the emperor Romanos saw how unbearable this hardship was, he made provision worthy of his compassionate charity and relieved the want caused by the famine with many alms. He had the porticoes of the colonnaded streets closed in with screens and planking, so that snow and cold could not get in on the poor there. He also built the so-called arklai, or shelters, in all the colonnades. He ordered that silver be given every month to the poor who lay there, and that the monthly trimisia be handed out to the poor in the churches. In all, the gifts to the poor in the shelters and in the churches came to twelve thousand in coined silver. His compassionate soul arranged all this out of care for the poor. He also ordered that three poor men should eat with him every day, and each of them received a nomisma. On Wednesdays and Fridays three poor monks ate with him and received the appointed nomisma. He also adopted the custom of the monasteries of reading aloud during meals. In this way he set a double table for himself and his guests: the body was fed with its usual food, while the soul was moved to compunction, and he shed floods of tears. He never met a monk devoted to virtue without confessing his deeds to him with many tears. [?] He adorned the churches of the city splendidly with fine sheer hangings and lamps. He also never failed to send every year the stipends he had fixed for the monks in the mountains, on Olympus, Kyminas and the mountain of Paracheion [?]. We have told these few things out of the many among his countless good deeds and acts of charity. Peter the Bulgarian was attacked by his brother John, together with other Bulgarians from Symeon's circle. They were found out. John was flogged and shut in prison, and the rest suffered severe punishments. When Peter made this known to the emperor Romanos, the emperor sent the monk John, who had held the rank of

rhaiktor. The stated purpose was to arrange an exchange of the prisoners held by each side, but in truth he was to seize John and bring him to Constantinople, and this is exactly what happened. The monk took John on board his ship at Mesembria and brought him to the City. Not long afterward John threw off the monastic habit and sought a wife. The emperor gave him a house and a great many estates, and a wife from his own homeland, the Armeniakon. He also held a splendid [?] wedding for him in the house of the Caesar. On the second of March a cornice on the columns of the Forum fell and killed six men. A great and terrible fire broke out in the colonnade of the Forum near the church of the most holy Mother of God, and the candle-makers' shops and the furriers' shops of the Forum burned down as far as the Psicha [?]. The emperor Christopher died in August of the fourth indiction, and his body was laid in his father's monastery mentioned above. In August of the third indiction they deposed the patriarch Tryphon. He went away to his own monastery and died there. The Church was left without a patriarch for one year and five months, because Theophylact, son of the emperor Romanos, was still too young. A certain Basil, a Macedonian impostor, proclaimed himself to be Constantine Doukas and drew many followers after him. He was arrested by Elephantinos, tourmarch of the Opsikion, and brought to Constantinople. There Peter the eparch had one of his hands cut off. Later [?] he went back to the Opsikion. He fitted a bronze hand in place of the one that had been cut off, had an enormous sword made, and went about deceiving many people into believing that he was Constantine, son of Doukas. He drew them after him and raised a great revolt against Romanos. The emperor sent an army against him and captured him and his followers. They brought him into the City, interrogated him, and beat him many times. He falsely accused many officials of being his accomplices, but he was proved to have said nothing true against them, and he was burned to death in the Amastrianon. The emperor's son Theophylact, mentioned earlier, was ordained patriarch on the second of February in the sixth indiction. Legates had come from Rome bringing a synodal decree concerning his ordination, and they installed him on the patriarchal throne. The emperor Romanos took a wife for his son Stephen named Anna. She was the daughter of [?] and the granddaughter of Katakylas. Together with the bridal crown she also received the crown of empire. The first campaign of the Turks against the Romans took place in April of the seventh indiction. They overran the land as far as the City and took captive

every soul in Thrace. The patrikios Theophanes, protovestiarios and chief minister, was sent against them, and the Turks themselves praised him highly for his prudence and good judgement. On that occasion the emperor Romanos showed his generosity and humanity, sparing no expense to ransom the captives. The emperor took a wife from the Armeniakon for his youngest son Constantine. Her name was Helena, and she was the daughter of the patrikios Adrian. When she died, he married him to another wife named Theophano. On the eleventh of June in the fourteenth indiction the Rus' sailed against Constantinople with ten thousand ships. The protovestiarios Theophanes was sent against them with triremes and dromons. He made the fleet ready in advance, secured it as well as he could, and waited for the Rus'. When they arrived and came near the Pharos, Theophanes was keeping watch at the mouth of the Black Sea, at the place called Hieron. He was the first to sail out in his own dromon. He broke up the formation of the Rus' ships and burned a great many of them with the prepared fire, and the rest were put to flight. The other dromons followed him out and completed the rout. They sank many ships together with their crews, killed many men, and took a great many alive. At that time John Kourkouas, the domestic, came down with the whole army of the East and destroyed many of the Rus', catching stragglers here and there. For they had done many evil things. They burned the district called Stenon. Of the captives they took, they crucified some and nailed others to the ground, and others they set up as targets and shot down with arrows. When they captured members of the priestly clergy, they tied their hands behind their backs and drove iron nails into the middle of their heads. They also set many holy churches on fire. Winter was already setting in and they had no food, so they decided to return home. They hurried to reach their ships, and in September of the fifteenth indiction they set out by night to sail across to the Thracian side. There they were met by Theophanes, for they could not escape his ever-watchful mind. At once a second sea battle took place, and he sank a great many ships. A few escaped with their ships, reached safety on the shore at Koile, and fled when night came. Theophanes returned with a brilliant victory, was received with honour, and was given the rank of parakoimomenos. Since John the magistros, mentioned earlier, proved outstanding in war, he extended the frontiers and sacked a great many cities of the Hagarenes

[?]-non (62). Because of the man's conspicuous virtue.... The patrician Pantherios, a relative of the emperor Romanos, was appointed domestic in his place. In the first indiction, in the month of April, the Turks attacked again with a very large force. The patrician Theophanes the parakoimomenos went out and made a peace treaty with them, that the peace should be kept for five years. In the second indiction the emperor Romanos sent Paschalios, protospatharios and strategos of Longobardia, to Hugh, king of Francia, seeking his daughter as a bride for Romanos, the son of his son-in-law Constantine; and the said Paschalios received her and brought her up to the City with great wealth. The marriage took place in the month of September; she died after living five years with her husband. In the days of the reign of Constantine, her father-in-law, a very violent wind blew down in the month of December, and the so-called "demes" in the Hippodrome fell (65) — those that stood opposite the imperial throne — and smashed the marbles beneath them, which are called "breasts". When the year had come round, in the same month, they brought the emperor Romanos down from the palace. While the city of Edessa, in which the precious imprint of Christ was kept, was being besieged by the Roman army and was reduced to the direst straits, its inhabitants sent envoys to the emperor Romanos, pleading for the siege to be lifted and promising to hand over the holy imprint of Christ. In return for such a favor they asked to receive in exchange captives from among their notables, and to receive a chrysobull guaranteeing that their territory would no longer be plundered by the Roman army; and this was done. When the holy imprint had been sent off and was already drawing near to Constantinople, Theophanes the patrician and parakoimomenos went out to the river Sangarios and met it with splendid honor and hymn-singing; and on the fifteenth of the month of August he entered the City with it, the emperor being at Blachernae and venerating it there. On the next day it went out to the Golden Gate; and the emperor's two sons, Stephen and Constantine, and his son-in-law Constantine, together with the patriarch Theophylact, received it with fitting honor, the whole senate going before it and a great procession of lights leading the way, and carried it on foot as far as the church of the Holy Wisdom of God; and after it had been venerated there, they brought it up into the palace. In those days a portent came to the City from Armenia [?]. Male children, joined together, from ... because of the man's conspicuous virtue, the emperor Romanos wished to take his daughter as a wife for his own grandson Romanos, the son of his son Constantine. But since envy was stirred up against him by the other emperors on account of this matter, he removed him from office, after he had served as domestic without interruption for twenty-two years and seven months. "The domestic, however" [?] in Cedrenus [?] which in Leo [?] "marbles called breasts".

who had come forth from one womb, complete in all the members of the body, but joined together from the pit of the stomach down to the lower belly, and facing each other. They spent a long time in the City, and since everyone looked on them as an extraordinary portent, they were driven out of the City as an evil omen. During the sole reign of Constantine they came back again. When one of them died, some skilled physicians deftly cut through the joined part in the hope that the other would live; but he survived three days and died. Now, as was said above, the emperor placed his trust in all monks, but above all he honored and revered Sergios, who shone among monks; he was the brother of the magistros Kosmas and the nephew of the patriarch Photios, and the emperor honored him more for the nobility of his soul than for that of his birth. The emperor kept this celebrated man with him constantly, as a true rule and plumb-line by which he always ordered his life. Sergios often urged the emperor to take care of his sons and not to leave them undisciplined and inclining to wickedness, lest he too should suffer the fate of Eli. And when his sons brought him down from the palace and exiled him to the island of Prote, he again had Sergios as a consolation in his misfortunes and a soothing remedy for his afflictions. With him at that time was also Polyeuktos, a most devout monk, who likewise offered him fitting consolation; when the patriarch Theophylact died, Polyeuktos was appointed patriarch by the emperor Constantine. But since God wills to save man in many ways, he allowed the emperor Romanos too to fall into unexpected misfortune, so that, chastened by it and brought to an awareness of his own transgressions, he might be found worthy of salvation. For he allowed his son Stephen to rise up against him, as Absalom once rose up against David, his own father. Stephen, using as his counselors for this the former monk Marianos, Basil Peteinos and Manuel Kourtikes, and with the other emperors also privy to it, wickedly brought him down from the palace, exiled him to the island of Prote and had him tonsured a monk. The sole reign of Constantine. So Constantine, his son-in-law, was left as sole ruler. He at once honored Bardas, the son of Phokas, with the dignity of magistros and appointed him domestic of the Schools, since over a long time he had often displayed his valor in war. Next he made Basil, surnamed Peteinos, patrician and great hetaireiarch; Marianos, of the family of the Argyroi, he stripped of the monastic habit and made patrician and count of the stable; and likewise Manuel, surnamed Kourtikes, patrician and droungarios of the watch. Not long afterward the just judgment of God overtook all three of them, as men who had acted outrageously against the Lord's anointed, laid hands [?] on him, and coveted the throne. For they were caught in treason, and each of them

ended his life by a most pitiable death. I shall set out their affairs more fully and in greater detail in the aforementioned (66) account. Forty days later, on the twenty-seventh of the month of January, Constantine grew suspicious of the emperor Stephen and his brother Constantine, fearing that they might do the same against him; and he reasoned, as was natural, that if they had not spared their own father, how would they spare him? So he entertained them at a banquet, and when they were already seated at table, with the food still in their mouths, the so-called Tornikioi, the patrician Marianos and the others who had been made ready for this seized them, brought them down from the palace, confined them on the nearby islands and tonsured them as clerics. A little later they asked to see their own father and came to the island of Prote; and when they saw him in the monastic habit they were overcome with unbearable grief. Their father wept over them and said: "I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me." Then they were exiled: Stephen to Prokonnesos, from Prokonnesos to Rhodes, and from Rhodes to Mitylene; Constantine to Tenedos and from there to Samothrace, where he plotted a revolt against his guards and was slain. Michael, the son of the emperor Christopher, he deprived of the imperial sandals and made a cleric. While the emperor Romanos was on the island, the patriarch Theophylact and Theophanes the patrician and parakoimomenos [?] took counsel to bring him back into the palace [?] ... called Diabolinos [?]; he subjected the plotters to unbearable flogging, and of some he cut off their noses and ears, set them on donkeys and paraded them through the middle of the City. On the fifteenth of the month of July, in the sixth indiction, the emperor Romanos died first [?] on the island (65), and his body was carried to the City and laid to rest in his own monastery. Here ends [?] the chronography of the emperors [?] ... of Leo the Grammarian, in the month of July, on the eighth, the feast of the holy great martyr Procopius, in the year [?], in the indiction [?].
